Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) moved the third reading of bill No. 101, to amend the Transport Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Experimental farms service.
IS. Central experimental farm, $633,787.
What is the reason for the increases this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: The increases are: salaries, $2,640; cost of living bonus and other items, $3,662; equipment, $2,065; supplies and materials, $2,185; feed, $1,535; travelling expenses, $2,340. That makes a total of $14,427.

As a rule the experimental farms are given up to experiments, but there

Supply-Agriculture
are some farms that are used for purposes of illustration to demonstrate to the farmers how they should carry on. I know it is difficult for an experimental farm to pay its own way, but I would like to know to what extent the central experimental farm accomplishes this. In other words, what is the income from the sale of different lines of produce from the farm. We have the cost of running the farm, but is there any way of separating experimental activities from other work that is done? If so, how do they come out in separating one from the other?

I doubt very much whether it is possible to separate them entirely. I have here the expenditures on the different activities. Most of these are experimental. Take this particular item of feed. There is an increase of $1,535 and I would assume that has something to do with the experience which farmers have had on all farms in the last year. Crops were poorer than usual and there has been an increase in the purchase of feed. That feed would be entirely used up in carrying on experiments in connection with live stock. In some years they may have a small surplus which is sold-fruit, vegetables, poultry and other commodities. These things are used in experimental work but there may be some products that are sold, though that is not the intention behind the work of the farm. It is not intended that the farm should be operated to make a profit.
I understand that.

You have losses if you do certain things on a farm, and you make a profit if you do certain other things, but I am afraid I have not the figures here. When the officials come we may be able to give that.
Could the minister not give us the total sales of farm products from the * central experimental farm last year? I understand that a certain number of cattle and hogs were sold.
I am not sure that I have the figures here at the moment.
They operate on a rather large scale.

I am afraid I shall have to ask the committee to wait until the officials come; I do not think I have them here. Let the item stand.
Item stands.
Experimental farms service.
Vi. Branch farms and stations and illustration stations, $1,396,776.

I should like information as to what has been accomplished at the
central experimental farm and the farm at Summerland with regard to the substance which it is hoped will be of benefit in dealing with the codling moth. It is known at the present time as D.D.T.

I think we can best utilize the time until the officials come by giving the committee a recital of what is being done in connection with a number of experiments on plants having to do with rubber, dandelion and that kind of thing, at the different farms. I have a review of it here. Questions were asked when I was before the committee last and I think if I put this on Hansard it will probably take up the time until my officials are here and I can answer these questions in detail.
Rubber. We have ten acres at Ottawa, and there are six hundred acres in Peterborough county, this larger area being financed by the Department of Munitions and Supply. We also have plots on almost every experimental farm across Canada. Some of these have been successful and others have not.
Dandelions. Six acres are being grown at Ottawa, and we also have plots on most of the experimental farms across Canada. In some cases we have obtained good stands, while in other cases the stands have been very poor, Some plots of dandelions were seeded in 1942 and the material was harvested and turned over to the national research council for [DOT] rubber extraction. Research has also been done as to species and strains, and the rubber evaluation is being done jointly by the science service of the Department of Agriculture and the national research council.
Wool research laboratory. This has been anticipated for a number of years as a field laboratory, not in any way to study uses, as that is being done by the national research council. The purpose of this field laboratory will be to study the evaluation of fibre in the fleeces, both before and after shearing, as a basis for our breeding work with Corriedales, Romnolets, and our high class imported Rambouillets. All these sheep are located in south western Saskatchewan and southern Alberta.
It has been agreed by the national research council, the Canadian national wool growers, and the Department of Agriculture, that Lethbridge is probably the most logical place for the location of this laboratory. The establishment of this laboratory will make possible a more intensive study of wool as a basis for breeding than has been possible in the extensive grading of fleeces in the wool growers' warehouse at Weston, Ontario, where fleeces are studied annually by a special wool
Supply-Agriculture

committee consisting of representatives of the national research council and dominion experimental farms.
Linseed varieties of flax. The standard varieties suited to western Canada are Bison and Redwing, both of which are susceptible to rust which has become more prevalent in recent years. A new rust-resistant strain has been registered under the name Royal, which is as heavy in yield as Bison and Redwing and is sufficient in resistance to rust so that the disease^ does not materially reduce the yield.
Some newer and even more promising strains of linseed flax are being produced at the central experimental farm to meet western conditions, and it is hoped that at least one of these may be multiplied in the near future to either take the place of Royal or to supplement it in rust areas.
Kapok. At the request of the national research council in 1942, a considerable tonnage of milkweed pods was collected with the aid of school children, largely in Carleton county, Ontario. These pods were matured and the floss was extracted by a small hand machine originated by the experimental farms service and the science service. This floss was turned over to the national research council for study as to its value to replace kapok in life belts and fliers' buoyant suits, and similar purposes. In every test it showed buoyancy and water-resisting qualities quite equal to that of first 'class kapok.
It is of interest to. note that the United States had similar results, and in order to guarantee an adequate supply of kapok substitute they entered into a contract with Doctor Boris Berkman of Chicago, who originated a special machine somewhat similar to a cotton gin for separating the milkweed floss from the seed. It is understood that the contract which the United States naval department entered into with Doctor Berkman called for 1,000,000 pounds of floss in 1943, 2,000,000 pounds in 1944, and 3,000,000 pounds in 1945.
The Department of Munitions and Supply at Ottawa have not signified any desire that the Dominion Department of Agriculture produce this material in quantity.
Rust-resistant grains. The cereal division at the central experimental farm, Ottawa, and through its staff at the dominion rust research laboratory, Winnipeg, is continuing to study the possibility of producing rust-resistant grains of all kinds, of superior quality and higher yields than those already discovered.
Two very promising new varieties of oats are in process of being multiplied for distribution, and these should be superior to Vanguard, which is a stem rust-resistant variety, and to Efban, which is a leaf rust-resistant

variety. These new varieties combine resistance to both forms of rust.
The experimental farm at Brandon is specializing in the development of new rust-resistant barleys, and already two new varieties that are exceedingly promising are being multiplied.
The experimental station at Swift Current, Saskatchewan, has developed a variety particularly adapted to the drought areas, namely Prospect barley, which is now so widely used in south western Saskatchewan and south eastern Alberta.
Sawfly-resistant wheats. The experimental station at Swift Current has for many years been studying the possibility of developing a high quality wheat which is of a solid stem character, hence not susceptible to loss from the sawfly.
Remarkable progress has been made, and two strains have been developed with quality comparable to that of marquis wheat but which will have very definite resistance to sawfly damage.
It is probable that in 1945 there may be some considerable volume of these two strains available for distribution. The staff engaged in rust-resistant laboratory work and plant breeding at Winnipeg consists of Mr. C. H. Goulden, agricultural scientist, Mr. J. N. Welsh, agricultural scientist, and Mr. R. F. Peterson, agricultural scientist, as well as junior assistants and seasonal student assistants. Work is being carried on right across the country in connection with these different products. Questions were asked about them at the time my estimates were before the committee previously, and I give this information now.

As I have to go to the banking and commerce committee, may I ask the minister whether there has been any extension of the research in regard to potato plant diseases in New Brunswick? I regret to -see that the amount to be voted for these branch farms and illustration stations again has been reduced. I assume, of course, that this is due to the stress of war expenditures, but it seems to me a bit ineffective to cut down the work and have just a skeleton operation. I refer to the question of poultry at the Fredericton station, where they have a poultryman in charge. He is a full-time man, and under ordinary circumstances I think has an assistant. Since the farm foreman has been superannuated I believe the poultryman has temporarily taken over the farm management, and the assistant is now carrying on, but he has only three hundred hens, and of course that is ridiculous having regard to the

Supply-Agriculture
size of the division, the housing capacity and so on. I wonder just why this work has been cut down to these skeleton proportions, though the cost remains approximately the same. It seems to me the staff and the quantum of the stock in hand could be'kept up if they are going to maintain the division in operation. The minister may not have this information before him at the moment, but perhaps at a later stage he will put on the record just what is the position.

Like the hon. member for
York-Sunbury, I have to go to the banking and commerce committee, but I should likg to say a word on this item. At page 97 of the report of the department, reference is made to the work carried on at some of the branch -stations, including Indian Head, with which I am particularly concerned. The minister has covered part of the ground I was going to ask him about, with respect to rust-resistant oats and other grain, but I notice quite a reduction in this item. I hope there will not be any reduction in the amount devoted to experimental work at these branch stations. In Saskatchewan we have two or three of these stations doing very excellent work, particularly the one at Indian Head. I was there last year and saw some of the grain with which they were experimenting, and I want to tell the minister I regret to see the decrease in this item. I hope that will not mean that the work of these experimental stations will be affected.

My understanding is
that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle wants a sort of break-down of the reduction in the cost of operating our branch farms, particularly at Indian Head?
Yes.

The position is that we have reduced the cost in our estimates this year by $8,010 in total salaries, $14,240 in wages and $38,251 in buildings and lands. The net reduction amounts to $37,438. Practically all those amounts were capital expenditures made last year under supplementary estimates. That is, the $38,000 in connection with buildings and lands was capital expenditure, and these other items cover wages which were occasioned by the fact that we were carrying on certain building activities. I understand there is no reduction in the actual work being done at any of these farms, including the one to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury referred a few moments ago. I -believe that at the Fredericton farm the same work is being carried on this year as was carried on last year.

A few days ago I happened to notice in one of the eastern newspapers an article outlining the great contribution to Canadian agriculture made by Doctor Newman, of the central experimental farm. . Of course I would not want to take away any of the credit due Doctor Newman, but I am sure he would be the first to say that credit also should be given to the staff of the branch farms. I have another reason for speaking this morning. I am extremely proud of the work being carried on at the Swift Current experimental station. As has been so often said in this house, it is an outstanding example of the use that can be made of the dominion experimental station set-up. I know of no farm in Canada that has contributed more to agriculture in the way of research work and the development of proper agricultural methods than has the experimental station at Swift Current.
As I said, I noticed in the article to which I referred that Doctor Newman was incorrectly mentioned as the originator of the sawfly-resistant wheat referred to this morning by the minister. I am sure he would approve my placing on record a brief history of just what occurred in connection with that very important development. Last year, 1943,
I believe the cost of sawfly damage in western Canada was approximately $30,000,000, and that is by no means the limit to which that particular pest could damage our western crops. So that you will see the importance of developing a sawfly-resistant wheat in order to overcome one of the hazards which confront the western farmer. The two strains the minister has mentioned had their origin in 1926. Mr. Kemp, now the assistant superintendent at the experimental station, who has made other valuable contributions to agriculture, happened to notice that certain varieties of wheat with solid stems were not damaged by the sawfly pest. This caused him to think there might be some possibility of a solution to the sawfly problem in the development of a hard-stemmed wheat. He began to experiment in the hope that a hardstemmed wheat might solve the difficulty. In 1937 a slightly more extensive programme was outlined to breed varieties that would be resistant not only to sawfli-es but also to stem rust. I think we in parliament should pay tribute to the men who accomplish these miracles, who find out the laws which govern these things, and do a work which is so beneficial to mankind.
In ordinary hollow-stemmed wheat the sawfly deposits its egg inside the stem when the plant is in the boot stage. The egg hatches and the
Supply-Agriculture

I should like to support what the hon. member for Swift Current
(Mr. Graham) has just said with respect to a matter I have mentioned on former occasions -the pay we are giving to the men who are doing experimental work in agriculture in Canada. These men have certainly not been given the pay to which they are entitled, and as a result we have lost to the United States, where they find better remuneration for their services, some of our best men engaged in experimental work. These men, as the hon. member for Swift Current has said, have rendered a real service to agriculture in Canada. The development of rust-resistant wheat in western Canada, for example, was one of the things they accomplished in a very short period of time, some three years. It was a development which meant millions of dollars to agriculture in Canada and to the Canadian economy as a whole. I strongly support the idea that the minister give serious consideration to seeing that the men engaged in this type of work are given better salaries and more honours than they have been given in the past.
The minister has mentioned certain experiments which are being carried on in Canada with respect to cereals, rubber and other agricultural products. Are experiments being made with a view to developing alfalfa of a variety which will have better seed setting properties than our present varieties have? I believe some work has been done along this line; perhaps the minister will give us particulars and indicate stating how far the experiments have gone. At present it is quite a gamble to grow alfalfa seed in Canada. In some years the seed will set, and then for two years there will be no seed. The production also varies tremendously from season to season. The development of a better variety of alfalfa is of tremendous importance not only to the areas where the seed is being produced but to the whole of Canada, because alfalfa is one of our main fodder crops in the feeding of live stock.
Mr. SE'NN: I would like to emphasize what the hon. member for Melfort, (Mr. Wright) has said about alfalfa. For years alfalfa has been one of our main fodder crops in Ontario, and I believe it has extended now to the western provinces. But unfortunately in the last few years there seems to be less alfalfa grown. There are a number of reasons for that. One, as the hon. member for' Melfort has stated, is the uncertainty of getting a crop of seed. One year you will have a good crop of seed and the next year the seed will not set at all. Experimental work should be undertaken to ascertain if possible why there-
Supply-Agriculture

is so much uncertainty. I think experiments should be conducted to see if the reason for that cannot be found. .
Again, alfalfa as a pasture crop is bad for bloating cattle. I notice in one of the reports of the Department of Agriculture a reference to certain experiments made in that connection on experimental farms, and to the good results obtained from a certain treatment of the cattle. In Ontario every year there is a great loss of cattle from bloating when, they have fed on alfalfa pasture, particularly the second cutting. Something should be done to see if that cannot be prevented.
There is another matter in regard to alfalfa which is important. Experiments have been conducted from time to time in the use of alfalfa and other legumes for silage. I believe experiments are being conducted at the central experimental farm in regard to using alfalfa for silage rather than corn. Will the minister make a statement on that? More attention should' be paid to the development of this crop than has been given to it in the past.

In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Melfort, and which he asked on a previous occasion, I would answer in this way. We are carrying on experiments at the experimental farm at Ottawa, also at Saskatoon and Swift Current, in .connection with alfalfa. These experiments are for the purpose of trying to produce varieties in which the seed will set to better advantage than in some of the varieties now being used. The hon. member for Haldimand also referred to this matter. The experiments up to date would suggest that probably the quality of the soil upon which the alfalfa is being produced has much to do with the setting of the seed. The experiments are not completed but are being continued and we are getting results which should be helpful. Any information that we gain from time to time is made available to farmers.

Are these experiments in the production of alfalfa seed being made at the illustration stations in northern Saskatchewan in the alfalfa seed producing areas? It seems to me that that would be the logical place. What have been the results obtained?
The experiments are being carried on at the illustration stations indicated, and the laboratory work is done at the agricultural college at Saskatoon.
Have any experiments been made with regard to bloating in cattle as a result of eating alfalfa?

Another question asked by the hon. member for Haldimand was with

regard to the use of alfalfa for ensilage. The experiments indicate that there is a higher protein content in ensilage from alfalfa than in ensilage from corn. Ensilage from alfalfa can be produced to better advantage if molasses is available. At present it is not available, but even without molasses the ensilage from alfalfa has a higher protein content.
With respect to bloating, the experiments that have been carried on indicate that there is no great danger from bloating if the stock are handled in the proper way, and are placed on the alfalfa when it is in its proper stage of development.
I think that has something to do with it.

I have fed cattle on clover and alfalfa in the west, and I found that if the cattle were shut off from water in the early part of the day they would bloat if allowed on clover with a heavy dew on it. The only time I have lost cattle on clover is through their not getting to water in the early part of the day. The experiments that are being conducted show that it is largely a matter of handling the cattle, rather than anything having to do with the alfalfa or clover itself.
At what illustration stations in northern Saskatchewan are experiments being carried on to develop a better seed setting variety of alfalfa?
Most of it is being carried on at the experimental station at White Fox, which I think is on the north side of the Saskatchewan river, just across from Nipawin.

I am always greatly interested in the estimates for experimental farms and for agriculture generally. I was particularly impressed to-day by the remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current, and I want to follow for a few minutes along somewhat the same lines, because I have often felt, as I believe we all have, that in the hurly-burly of the present day we pay very little heed to the men and women of ability and vision who laid so well the local foundations of many parts of this dominion; men and women whose philosophy of life consisted of deeds of service rather than of words.
With this introduction I want to make a few remarks regarding some men who took a leading part in the founding of experimental farms in western Canada. I have in mind three men particularly, only one of

Supply-Agriculture
whom is still living. That one is Mr. A. C. Fraser, of Brandon. Born at White Lake in the county of Renfrew, Ontario, Mr. Fraser, although now in his ninety-fifth year, is just about as mentally alert as any hon. member of This house. I had the pleasure of visiting with him a few months ago, and I may say that I do not think there is any hon. member who can give a better appraisal of the qualities of the members of our cabinet than can Mr. Fraser, although he has seen only one of them, the Prime Minister. I want to say in passing that the Minister of Agriculture, whose estimates are being considered to-day, seems to be a special favourite of this old gentleman. I have heard in my day, in this parliament and out of it, some very fine speakers, but rarely have I heard one endowed with as great a gift of eloquence as Mr. Fraser possessed in his palmy days, making him one of the outstanding speakers of Canada. He was mayor of Brandon in the early years, and recalls with much satisfaction the urge he made to have experimental farms established in western Canada and his insistence that one of those farms be located at Brandon. That farm is now recognized as one of the most [DOT] iseful and beautiful in western Canada.
A second pioneer to whom I wish to refer in connection with Brandon experimental farm is the late Senator W. D. Perley, whose son so ably represents the constituency of Qu'Appelle, which adjoins my own. The late Senator Perley was born in New Brunswick, but came as a young man to northwestern Canada, settling near what is now known as Indian Head. His work was soon recognized in the fact that he was elected to represent Indian Head riding in the Northwest Council, corresponding to the provincial legislature before Saskatchewan became a province. He was afterwards elected to the federal parliament, and served here until called to the senate. It was during his membership in the House of Commons that Mr. Perley was chosen as one to select those experimental farms, and the fine judgment he showed on that occasion is evident in the splendid locations of various farms in northwestern. Canada.
Then there is another who, more than anyone else, contributed to the .development of the Brandon farm. I refer to one whose name will be recalled and revered by some of the older staff of the agriculture department, the late Doctor S. A. Bedford, who also took an active part in selecting its location. Like so many contributors to the upbuilding of Canada, Doctor Bedford was born in England but came to this country when quite a young man. He remained for a time in Ontario, but in the spring of 1877 set out for
the 'west. He ultimately took up land in the constituency so ably represented to-day by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler) and the experimental, farm at his home town, Morden, remains one of the finest to be found in all Canada. Doctor Bedford, in addition to superintending farming operations, surveyed large tracts of country for the dominion government and acted in an advisory capacity for several land companies. These duties necessitated his going farther west, and he took up residence in what is now Moosomin, Saskatchewan. At that time Moosomin was not even included in any electoral division. Doctor Bedford was requested to lay out such a division, and he wTas elected by acclamation as its first member and served for two terms in the Northwest Council. He later was appointed first superintendent of the Brandon experimental farm, and he converted that ordinary prairie piece of land into what is now a thing of beauty and a joy forever. His son. Mr. H. B. Bedford, is one of the leading residents and most respected citizens of Brandon.
I had the privilege a few years ago of attending a function in Doctor Bedford's memory, held at the entrance to a beautiful shaded driveway leading from the highway to the farm buildings. The occasion was marked by the unveiling at the entrance of that driveway of a substantial bronze plaque, on which are inscribed these words:
"Bedford Drive, named in honour of Doctor S. A. Bedford, the First Superintendent of Brandon Experimental Farm 1888 to 1906."
It was a quiet function, but it was a sincere tribute by his friends to the memoiy of a sterling man. There before us were the fruits of his labour-the fertile fields sloping southwards to the Assiniboia river, the herds of pure bred cattle, the poultry houses and the colonies of bees, the trees, the shrubberies, the lawns, a landscape of rare scenic beauty. In looking over these grounds I have felt that the ppet Kipling and Doctor Bedford had much in common. One expressed his thoughts in words, the other in deeds:
Our country is a garden that is full of stately views
Of borders, beds and shrubberies, and lawns and avenues,
With statues on the terraces, and peacocks strutting by,
But tile Glory of the Garden lies in more than meets the eye.
I make no apology, Mr. Chairman, for taking up a little of the time of this house to pay my tribute to these three noble men, Mr. A. C. Fraser, the late Senator Perley and the late Doctor Bedford-not perhaps that they are more deserving than hundreds of others of the pioneers of western Canada, but

Supply-Agriculture

because their duties, being of a public nature, came more directly under the public eye. These are the type of men, scoffers notwithstanding, who have built up this country and made it what it is to-day, the type of men whom doubtless the poet had in mind when, after referring to the material greatness of the west he issued this appealing call:
Bring us men to match our mountains, Bring us men to match our plains.
Bring us men to match our prairies And new eras in their brains.

I should like to support
the hon. members for Swift Current and Brandon in what they have said as to the value of experimental substations. I will give a concrete example. Over seven years ago a substation was set up in our district and I was told then by somebody who pretended to know that it was an outstanding waste of money. This person was running a small store and not making a success of it and he said that the farmers of the district knew all there was to know about their farms. However, the farmers were willing to learn and a substation was set up. A young man was put in charge of it and it was established on a firm basis. I may say that he resigned from his position to join the air force and made the supreme sacrifice, so that that farm is now a memorial to him. There is a field day every year and the farmers and their wives as well as city folks come to see what is done on the farm. They see what can be produced on the three types of soil to be found on the farm. They see the value of fertilizer in the growth of small fruits suitable to the different types of soil. They see what can be done with wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and grasses, and what can be done by cultivation and the proper use of fertilizers. I know' that some work is being done, such as the rebuilding of dikes destroyed in 1943. There is one other matter about which I should like to get information, namely, the establishment of a much-needed animal disease research laboratory in the maritime provinces. I should like to make a statement in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Yale with regard to the codling moth.
The codling moth is becoming an increasingly serious pest in all the apple growing regions of Canada. It is now the most important orchard pest in the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia, where eventual elimination of the industry is threatened unless effective economic control is soon developed. Two very promising projects are being pursued at
the Vernon laboratory. These involve the destruction of the moths by toxic sprays, and the control of overwintering larvae by special dormant applications to the tree trunks of sprays consisting of oil solutions of dinitro-cresol. In general spray practice particular emphasis is being placed on the use of arsenical substitutes. In the warmer parts of Ontario there are two broods of codling moth and the insect is the most serious source of loss to apple growers; pears, too, are affected. Present investigations include improvement of the spray programme, adoption of supplementary measures, and the development of biological control, chiefly by parasites. Until a few years ago the codling moth was not of importance in Nova Scotia orchards. It has increased since then and is locally a severe pest. Both there and in Quebec investigations are in progress to establish improved control practices.

I am sorry I did not take part in the discussion when the matter of alfalfa was brought to the attention of the minister by the hon. member for Haldimand, but I should like to say that in my opinion this is one of the most important matters to be discussed this morning in connection with agriculture in my section of the country. Alfalfa has become one of the most impor-tants crops in Canada. I well remember that in my youth it was a common thing to get seed from the second crop of alfalfa, and there was seldom if ever a failure.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that statement meets with the approval of the hon. member. I am inclined to the view that we are having difficulty to-day because we have followed the recommendation of the department and changed the variety of alfalfa we were growing. Formerly we grew what was known as Ontario Variegated, and we were advised to change to the Grimm variety. The old Ontario Variegated had its disadvantages, of course. One was that it was a coarse, deep-rooted variety which was hard to plough. To-day, however, with tractors to do the ploughing, that disadvantage is not so important. It also grew perhaps somewhat coarser, provided you did not cut it in time, but I have never had the same success since I have been growing the Grimm variety. I am rather inclined to believe that while experiments undoubtedly are necessary, they do not always bring about improvements. I think it was Charles Dickens who had Sam Weller say, when he married the second time, that changes are not always improvements. I have not seen any of the Ontario

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to note a slight increase in the estimate, but I would be more pleased if it were still greater.
A number of us have been worried for some time in connection with veterinary services for agriculture. In years gone by we have suffered from low live stock prices, with the result that there were many times when it was difficult for the farmer to pay for veterinary services required for his animals. Consequently many of the young men who would have followed the veterinary profession did not do so. They either went somewhere else, or engaged in some other type of occupation. The result is that in many parts of western Canada with which I have been familiar for a long time the veterinary services at our disposal are strictly limited. In fact one could travel in some areas hundreds of miles where there are thousands upon thousands of live stock but no facilities for veterinary services. This condition has a bearing upon the future health of the human population.
The veterinaries working under the Department of Agriculture are to be complimented on the efficient service which they have given in the years gone by. We are indeed blessed that that service has been kept up to the extent that it has been through succeeding administrations. The dominion veterinarians, commonly referred to in many parts of the country as the dominion vets, have always been looked upon as men who knew their business and attended to their business. But to-day in many parts of the country the only veterinaries are those who are working for the Department of Agriculture. They have their own work to do, and the result is that the people generally cannot get veterinary service for their live stock.
On page 62 of the estimates, under health of animals, a break-down is given of the veterinary service, showing veterinary inspectors, associate chief veterinary inspectors and so on. I would ask the minister what is the average age of the men in this service, how many of them are in line for retirement within a short time, and what steps is the department taking to have young men trained to fit into these positions that will be becoming vacant-because I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that at least in my part of the country there is very little opportunity to replace these men from among the profession.
I would also ask a question which I believe is related to this vote. It really comes under
the Meat and Canned Foods Act. Many of us appreciate the splendid service which the department has given in the inspection of meats at the slaughtering plants and packing houses. Beef and pork coming through these plants are properly inspected, but while we are spending a considerable amount of money to see that meat is properly inspected, I believe that we are doing only half the job. While beef and pork are inspected, there is no proper inspection of poultry going through these packing plants. They have the poultry there, feathered but not drawn, and they are graded, and that is all the inspection of poultry that takes place. Coming down to the city here on a long trip one often meets people and discusses things with them. This last winter I had the opportunity of talking to a man who has been working for a number of years in a packing plant where they handle an enormous amount of poultry. Knowing what we have to contend with both as raisers and consumers of poultry, and particularly to see that diseased birds are not consumed, I asked this man what sort of inspection took place in this packing plant. He told me that all they could go by was this, that if a bird measured up to certain qualifications as being a finished bird, you usually could judge that that bird was not diseased. I said, and he agreed with me, that that was not an absolutely safe bet, that sometimes you would find a bird which, although apparently well finished, would be too much diseased to be safe for human consumption. He told me that the only safeguard which the consumers had was to buy high-grade poultry. I asked him what they did with the rest of the birds at the packing plant. He just grinned and said, "We put them into cold storage and later on we sell them out to some of the cheaper restaurants."
Any man who is familiar with poultry will know the number of diseases that are to be found in the ordinary flocks of poultry if they are not well taken care of, and even in some of the best taken care of flocks. While we inspect beef and pork passing through the slaughtering houses and packing plants, we allow diseased birds to be put into cold storage and later sold to the public. That is doing only half the job when it comes to inspecting the health of animals in its relation to the health of human beings.
We are indeed concerned that steps should be taken to continue to give us the efficient veterinary services that we have had under the Department of Agriculture, and also that steps be taken to ensure that young men will be trained to prepare themselves to carry on this important work.

I should like some information as to the general set-up of the health of animals branch. Having been in personal contact with the department for twenty-three years, I am prepared to say that I believe this is one of the most efficient branches of the agricultural service that we have, and one which has contributed a great deal to the general welfare and well-being not only of live stock but of individuals. The maintenance of good healthy live stock will promote better conditions of health in human beings. If the department is to retain the confidence of those who are most closely associated with it, the live stock producers of this country, it is essential that nothing that is necessary to make the department successful be overlooked. It is perhaps a delicate subject, but I have sometimes wondered whether, in the appointments by the civil service commission to the health of animals branch, veterinary workers who have had a great deal of experience in more subordinate positions are always chosen. For instance, when such a position as that of chief veterinary inspector becomes vacant, I am not sure that every effort is made to get the man best qualified to give direction to those whose business it is to give directions under his control. A certain amount of latitude must of course be allowed to those responsible for making the selection of these officers, but it is well that officials of the department, and in particular the health of
fMr. Burton.]
animals branch, should know that the type of farmer who is interested in the branch is the pure bred live stock farmer, who repre*-sents in large measure the very best element of the farmers,, the men who are sincerely interested not . only in maintaining production but in producing something which will improve the quality of live stock and the health of animals. These men take considerable interest in appointments affecting this branch, and sometimes they wonder whether the principle of merit is ignored, in that men who have had experience and have been giving direction are occasionally displaced by junior officers with less experience. The farmer keeps a pretty close eye upon the administration of this particular branch.
I do not know that it is up to me to offer any recommendations as to what the civil service commission should do with regard to making these appointments, but we believe that merit should be the title to any promotion, and it has been somewhat difficult for some of us to understand why some men who have filled subordinate positions should be pitchforked over the heads of others who have taken a responsible part in the administration of the branch and the carrying on of its work. I am inclined to think that sometimes a man can be so faithful in a position which calls for hard work that he is kept in that subordinate position because it is a hard job and is not allowed to reap the reward of his efforts and attain a position which would give him some of the credit and reward to which his work entitles him.
I hope I have made myself clear. I am not finding particular fault with the type of men who have been administering the branch, because we have had some splendid men in this particular department. All I want the department to know is that the farmer is interested in the work of the branch and looks with some surprise at some of the things which have been done. I understand that the civil service commission can easily give an answer, but that answer will not satisfy the average farmer. Maybe we are the silent partners in this business, but we observe what is going on. We trust the civil service commission to make appointments, but I am not sure that they are always wise in appointments they make.

The hon. member for Brant has drawn to the attention of the minister the health of animals, particularly cows; but I wonder whether it has been drawn to the minister's attention that protection should be given to animals against the human race. At least it was news to me this year when I read

a statement made by Doctor W. R. Gunn, who said in Victoria before the agriculture committee of the legislature:
It's not always the cow that's to blame when human being are infected with undulant fever or septic sore throat and other ailments common in dairying districts and among people who drink their milk raw.
Doctor W. R. Gunn, 11.C. live stock commissioner, told the agriculture committee of the legislature to-day that humans are too prone to blame the cow for prevalance of the infection known among humans as undulant fever and among dairy animals as Bang's disease. . . .
"It is possible that human beings may carry the organism of undulant fever around in their blood and if they come in contact with cows, infect them," he said.
"We know that has been the case with tuberculosis. We had one case of a sanitarium herd which we did everything to clean up but we got no results until we traced the T.B. to one of the dairy workers. Similarly with septic sore throat.
"That is definitely a human organism and if some dirty human comes in contact with a herd, the cows get it and are consequently blamed when it is transmitted to other humans."
That is most interesting, especially in view of the fact that we have a farm population of some three million people, with a permanent hired man population of 64,130. Has the minister had that brought to his attention, and if so, have representations in this regard been made by his department to the health branch?
