A number of matters have been spoken of. The first is the question of promotions within the department, particularly promotions which are related to the health of animals branch. I have only to say that the same practice is followed in respect of promotions in the health of animals branch as is followed throughout the department and elsewhere in the service. The matter of seniority has something to do with it. That is, provided the qualifications are the same, seniority of course would count. The particular positions which were discussed by the hon. member for Brant are positions to which both of those qualifications apply. On one occasion when the gentleman in question was under consideration it was a matter of appointing the man who had seniority in the department as well as considering qualifications which were at least equal to those of others who were available for the position. For the position under consideration at present, the same study will be given to qualifications as was given on previous occasions and selections will be made accordingly.
The hon. member for Humboldt this morning raised a question as to the possibility of filling positions in the department as a result of graduations of veterinarians from different colleges in Canada. I can answer his question best by saying that we have now in the employ of the department 383 veterinarians, though we should have a few more. Our staffs are not fully manned at present because there are great demands upon them in consequence of the increased production of hogs and the present arrangements made in connection with the marketing of beef and so forth. That all requires more men than we have had in the past, and we could use more if they were available. Generally, we require about 25 men each year to take care of replacements. I think this fully answers the questions asked as to how many men go out each year, how many come in, how many we have on the staff and so on. We have only two veterinarian colleges in Canada, one at Guelph, and the other at Oka in the province of Quebec, and from these a year ago there were 41 graduations. This year there will be 19 and next year we expect there will be more; that is, we anticipate a larger number, but of course the students still have to go through their courses.
These figures on the average would probably take care of our requirements if there were no other demands to be met. I pointed out this morning that live stock is worth more now than before the war. There is much more of it and there is a greater demand for
Supply-Agriculture

veterinarian services than there was a few years ago, and that may have some bearing on the question of salaries, though not so much as might appear on the surface. The salaries of all civil servants are compared right through the service from time to time by the civil service commission. As a matter of fact it is impossible for me to get anyone put on in the Department of Agriculture anywhere, even outside the civil service as that is generally understood. It is difficult to get any man engaged in the department without referring the matter to the civil service commission.
Can you not get temporaries?

Not even temporaries.
The general rule is that they must be submitted to the civil *ervice commission, not on the question whether they will be hired or not but on the question of qualifications as compared with others receiving comparable salary for a similar position. Comparisons must be made with salaries paid in other parts of the civil service, and of course there is the further consideration as to whether a man is going to a job that will last only three or four months, for which there is no superannuation, or whether he is going to take on work that will be permanent, carrying superannuation at the end of a certain period. All these factors must be considered, but an attempt is made to keep the services given in one department paid on a level comparable with the services in another and throughout the department in question. On that basis the salaries paid to veterinarians are possibly the same as salaries paid to others for comparable work, and while I would be most anxious to see those in my department paid higher salaries than at present, I would suggest that in order to get them paid higher salaries it would probably be necessary to have higher salaries paid throughout the other services.
They do however benefit from the cost of living bonus?

Yes. This morning certain persons were mentioned, I believe, by the hon. member for Swift Current. One of those mentioned in the group of three would be a person who would have received an increase had it not been for the war. There is however a general regulation at present whereby increases are not given except under restricted circumstances. But cost of living bonuses are paid, and while salaries have not gone up, the bonus in some cases is paid on a basis which gives a higher return than is indicated by the mere salary itself. The position is related to

the other question we were discussing, whether veterinarians can keep themselves in employment in different parts of the country in peace time. The condition was different in peace time from the present condition, as the member for Humboldt understands. For a time the price of live stock was low, and a person would think many times before sending a considerable distance for a veterinarian, but today the situation is different. If veterinarians were available in certain areas they would undoubtedly be called much more often than the farmers can get them at the present time. The situation that exists to-day has its effect on salaries. Salaries are not as high as they might have been. In other words, men were quite satisfied to take a job in the department at a salary rather than try to practise outside. All these factors are considered, but the chief factor is the relationship between officials in the department and between those in the department and officials in other departments.

Is the cost of living bonus written into the salaries of civil servants as it is into the wages of those working in industry?
Mr. GAR-DINER: It is not written into the salaries. Every time I am asked for an explanation of increases I have given the increase resulting from salary, which means that there is a legal increase that does take place in some cases, and in addition to that there is the increase that comes about as a result of the cost of living bonus.
Why is the cost of living bonus not included in the salaries of civil servants just as it is in wages paid in industry?
The theory is that the whole matter is to be considered at the end of the war in relation to conditions then existing.

This is an important branch of the department. The minister has made an interesting statement with regard to veterinary inspectors, of whom he says there are 383 in the department. Looking over the annual report of the department I see on page 106 a statement with reference to orders in council that have been passed establishing restricted areas in connection with bovine tuberculosis. In Saskatchewan twenty-two new municipalities came in within the period covered by this report. There are 300 odd municipalities in that province and I would like the minister to make a statement as to the number that have come in. I notice from this report that certain municipalities are withdrawing from the restricted areas. Why would that be? On the following page there is a table of the per-

Supply-Agriculture
centage of inspected slaughterings in each province to the total for all Canada. It shows that Saskatchewan has almost the lowest of any, only 6-26 per cent of the slaughterings of cattle. Could the minister give us an idea of the comparative health of animals in each province? May we take this percentage of inspected slaughterings in the annual report as an indication of the health of animals in western Canada?

In answer to the last question, the experience has been that the number of reactors to tuberculosis in western Canada is lower than the number in eastern Canada. That, of course, would be due to different conditions which I do not think I need to enumerate to the committee.
Has climate anything to do with it?

Climate may have, but I would think that one thing that has as much to do with it as anything else is the fact that we have not had live stock there as long as other places, and our foundation stock when it was taken out there was probably checked. We have not had live stock there as long as they have had them in other sections. Then, the way in which live stock is housed has something to do with it as well. Quite a number of considerations enter into it, but the fact is there is less tuberculosis on the prairie provinces than in the other provinces.
With regard to the other question, as to tuberculosis areas going in and out, I understand that there are no districts that have ever been organized as anti-tuberculosis areas that have disorganized and gone out. There are districts in which we did have tuberculosis free herds, accredited herds, and those have been disorganized in some cases because the whole district has come under the tuberculosis act. I understand that when once a district comes under the act there is no way in which it can disorganize.
Is it not compulsory under the act to have further inspection at certain periods?

That is quite true. The district has to be rechecked every so often in order to keep it in good standing; but there is a possibility that if the district were not checked over a period of years the herds in that area would not be in good standing.
My understanding is that the act compels that check within a certain period. If inspectors are not available, what happens to the district?

If inspectors were not available and it was found impossible to carry
on the inspection for a period of time, people would refuse to accept stock out of that area as being free from tuberculosis. I may have some figures in regard to that. That, if it happened, would be the responsibility of the department, and perhaps a responsibility that the department could not discharge, because of the difficulty for the time being of getting veterinarians in to do the job.
What would happen then?
What happens when cattle are sold for export? Is there not a special provision in cases of the kind?

If they come from an area that is in good standing, they are permitted to go direct. If the district is not in good standing, they must be checked within thirty days of the time they come to the boundary line.
Would the minister give us the number of areas or rural municipalities that are in the restricted area, and also the number of inspectors that are operating in Saskatchewan out of the 383?

There are fifty-five
municipalities in Saskatchewan. The numbers and names are here.
That is not very many out of some three hundred municipalities.
No, it is not so many.
How many inspectors are there in the area?
These are the certified districts; some others have been inspected but not yet certified.

I am seeking information, and I am not yet clear on it. Let us presume that a district in British Columbia is in an accredited area and inspectors are not available. What happens to that district? What happens to a district that wants to continue in the area but cannot get inspectors within the period?

All that happens is this. I know it is an inconvenience to some people, but anyone who wishes to ship cattle out of that area into an anti-tuberculosis area or into the United States would have to have his cattle tested by a veterinarian somewhere within thirty days of the time that they are shipped.

What is the position in New-Brunswiek; is it entirely within the line?
Supply-Agriculture
New Brunswick is all in. All the maritimes are in.

That is very interesting, and I am glad to hear it. How many inspectors are available in New Brunswick? How many veterinarians are there on the staff in New Brunswick? I think there used to be one at McAdam, on the border, and one at Fredericton, but I am not sure.
I should have said, all the maritimes with the exception of Cape Breton.
It is not yet clear to me.
Just a minute until I get this information.

I started it; let me finish it. I am not quarrelling with this matter, but I cannot see why a certain area in British Columbia that is accredited but cannot get inspectors should be penalized when shipping out or elsewhere. I mat be mistaken, but I think I am correct and that it is happening in British Columbia to-day.

You would not be
penalized other than to this extent: no one would accept your cattle unless they had been inspected, and you would have to have them inspected within thirty days of the time they are shipped out. Suppose, as an example, you are living on the edge of any of those districts or areas. You are not allowed to buy cattle from your first neighbour just across the road and bring them into the area without test. Anyone who brings them in there has to have them tested within thirty days of the time they are brought in, and that, is the restriction which compels anyone in a district which has not been checked up to date to have them checked individually if he desires to ship any out within that period of time.
How often have these cattle to be tested in a restricted area? Is it once a year, or once every two years? When do they lose their accredited standing?

If they are below one-half of one per cent. They are certified for a three year period, sometimes it is six years, sometimes it is longer. The periods are three, six and nine years. There are nine veterinarians in New Brunswick.
What are the new areas in Ontario? I understand that several places have been petitioning to be accredited, but have not yet received it.

At the beginning of the war we were pressing forward the checking of

the districts in Ontario. The reason for that was that we had a good trade developing between this country and the United States, and we were most anxious that all the districts out of which shipments were going should be checked as soon as possible. We were working back gradually from the United States boundary line into the north country, to try and get the situation cleaned up. After the war came on, for a short time we almost discontinued the policy, but finally took the position that it should be continued wherever necessary in order to round out a district. We made an exception of some of the areas in Ontario from which breeding stock in particular was being exported to the United States; we tried to cover those districts as quickly as possible. Then we were trying to round out counties or, in the west, municipalities which were hedged in by others, where difficulties would arise because you could not move cattle back and forth across the boundary lines. We have been trying to round out those areas in order to remove that difficulty as much as possible. We have followed the practice of taking them in the order in which applications are received and put through.
Does the first move have to come from the locality?
Yes. A petition comes in from the district, which must be signed by two-thirds of the people concerned.
In other words there is a sort of local option. Has the government ever given consideration to making it compulsory? It is such a good thing it seems to me it should be compulsory.
I suppose we might have that when we get to the time when most of the country is covered.

Perhaps
that is asking too much.
At the moment I think it is.

I should like to refer particularly to the county of Haliburton, which I think could be classed as one of the areas described by the minister. It is surrounded by accredited areas, such as Peterborough, Victoria on the south and Ontario on the west. These are all accredited districts. The county of Haliburton is a stocker producing county with a comparatively small cattle population. Very few cattle are finished and sent to market from this county. In the fall of the year conditions become congested, and I am sure the local veterinaries and any assistants they are able to secure have more work than they can

Supply-Agriculture
handle. Would it be possible to have that small area included now, in order to round out the district? I cannot give the exact cattle population-
It is eight thousand. The matter is under consideration, but we are not working in there yet.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter having to do with the sale of hogs in Ontario; I do not know whether or not the same conditions exist in other provinces. Since the system of rail grading of hogs has been in force in Ontario the packing companies have been deducting one-half of one per cent of the value of the hogs as condemnation insurance, to compensate for hogs condemned as unfit for human consumption by the inspectors of the health of animals branch. In 1942-43 something tike two million hogs were marketed in Ontario, and under this condemnation insurance the packing companies deducted something over 8200,000, yet I understand that in the same period only about three thousand hogs were condemned which, at $25 a head, \yould amount to $75,000. In addition, parts of these condemned hogs were used, so they were not a total loss. I should like to know from the minister if his department has any check or control over the packing companies who deduct this very large sum of money from the returns of the farmers, and whether the packing companies make any accounting in connection with it.

This matter was discussed when my estimates were last before the committee. I do not know how we got to it, but just the same it was discussed. As I stated then, this is not a fund set up by the department, and it has no relationship to the rail grading of hogs. It has been in existence since about 1907, or in any case since early in the century.
There must be some authority for it.

It was an arrangement entered into by some representatives of the producers, perhaps by swine breeding associations, and the packing plants under which the packers are permitted to take one-half of one per cent of the value of the hogs delivered. There is an impression, I believe, that a fund was created. No fund has been created. The packer simply deducts one-half of one per cent of the value of the hogs he buys, and whenever there are any losses he pays them. The question that arises from time to time is whether he deducts more
than he actually pays out. It has been suggested that the department should take some responsibility in the matter and require an accounting in connection with that fund So far no action of that kind has been taken.
I am not certain in my own mind as to whether it would be a proper thing for the department to do. I understand an investigation was held some two years ago by a number of counties in Ontario, and my understanding is that it was generally considered by those who carried on that investigation that the fee was reasonably taking care of the losses, which were paid by the packing houses. That is my memory of the finding, that no one was making any considerable amount of money out of it.
It applies to cattle too, does it not?

Yes, it does. So far as we can make out from the investigations that have been held, the one-half of one per cent pretty well takes care of the losses. Some people argue that they have sent in stock for a long time and had this one-half of one per cent taken off their returns, but they have had no losses and they want to know what has become of their money. That is the argument made from time to time in connection with any form of insurance. A person who never has a fire never draws anything, and in this case the man who never happens to have a hog condemned does not receive anything in return. However, that was the theory when it was started; that when you dumped the hogs of four or five or a dozen farmers into one car and two of them happened to be condemned as a result of some ' disease, the one farmer should not take the whole loss.

The minister said this system of deducting one-half of one per cent came into effect some time around 1907. He will remember, however, that before the system of rail grading came into operation, when a drover bought and took delivery of hogs, they were then the property of the drover and he was responsible for making delivery to the packing house and therefore responsible for anything that happened in transit. I understand that this fund does not compensate for any injury or damage to hogs while in transit from the farms to the packing houses. It is used only for the purpose of covering hogs that are condemned by the inspectors as unfit for human consumption after they are slaughtered. Will the minister say whether or not that is correct?-because I took from his remarks of only a moment ago that it covered hogs damaged in transit.
Supply-Agriculture
That is what he did say.

Of course there is a difference in the marketing as compared with forty years ago. I think probably the hon. member is right when he says that all the hogs, or nearly all of them at that time, were taken in by drovers, and it was most difficult to follow the hogs back to the original owners. That difficulty does not exist to-day, because, the hogs are marked and they can be followed back to the owners.
They are mostly trucked.

Yes, and it is possible that a change in plan could be made, or a new method of payment could be set up. However I am just saying that what has happened up to date is as I have pointed out. There is just the possibility that someone-whether it be a meeting of producers and packers, or whether it should be done through the department-could devise a plan under which hogs could be followed back. I am not just sure where that would get you. I am not sure whether the people who are asking for this think that a man should take the loss on his own hogs. I should think however that that would be questionable, because if one were to put 50 hogs in one group in a car, and for some reason one or two of those hogs were killed, and they happened to belong to one man, I cannot see any reason why that man should carry the loss and the others should be allowed to go free.

Has the minister ever looked into the legality of this procedure of the packing companies making deductions? The minister said his department has nothing to do with it. I am asking him if the packers have any legal right to make those deductions.

I think we are probably confusing two things. First of all there is the matter of insurance on hogs killed in transit. I am assuming the reference here has been to diseased hogs which have been taken into plants and destroyed because of their having been diseased.

I think that is the whole point. I am advised by people who certainly know what they are talking about that under the present system when a farmer sells his hogs they remain his property until they reach the packing house, and that if those hogs are damaged or injured in a railway car or truck or other vehicle he must suffer the loss because they are his hogs until they reach the packing plant. This one-half of one per cent which is deducted by the packing

companies has nothing to do with compensation for hogs damaged in transit; it is for the purpose of paying for hogs condemned by inspectors from the minister's department. Would the minister comment upon that?
Mr. Chairman, if I might say-
Just a moment; let the minister answer.

May I not add something? This compensation was originally recommended by the swine breeders association of Canada. I am just drawing attention to that fact, because I happen to know it. This recommendation, like many others which have been made to. the department, can be traced back. Despite the fact that hog grading was condemned by many farmers, it was recommended by those who were most interested in the breeding of swine, and those people were in the swine breeders association. There is a long story there which I believe the people would find most interesting.
Would the minister give me an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the minister
answers, may I point out that we are discussing item 16, which deals with the health of animals. I doubt very much if this discussion is in order. Of course I am just giving my own impression.

It is my submission that this is the one item under which the matter to which I have referred could be discused. The hogs which are condemned would, I should think, come under the health of animals branch. The minister has indicated that he is willing to have the discussion take place on this item.

The point has been raised as a matter of health. When we began the discussion I thought it would be related to marketing, but I believe it may properly be discussed here.
The fund which has been mentioned is not in fact a fund. The packers simply pay less for all the hogs which come in. They pay one-half of one per cent less for all hogs coming in. The diseased hog is bought at its full value, and the farmer is paid the same for that hog as for any other. Then the hog is condemned, and the matter becomes one of health inspection and that particular animal is lost. That is the principle on which it operates. The farmer who owned the hog in the first instance is paid on exactly the same basis as is every other farmer.

Supply-Agriculture

But it has no legal sanction. It is just a custom which has grown into something approaching a law. As I understand it, the theory among the farmers is that the packers make a profit out of it, and that they are not rendered accountable to anybody. I do not think that is a proper situation. With regard to transportation, these hogs are transported by common carriers who must have some responsibility. What is the position in Ontario where the hogs are carried by truckers? Do they not have to insure?
They are required to.

With
respect to accidents on railway cars, there must be times when the railway companies will have legal responsibility. The matter ought to be reviewed.

They do have responsibility. The position is just as has been outlined. The hogs are insured against accident, and that was where I was confusing the matter in the earlier discussion. Those hogs are insured against accident, but my understanding on the other question is that each time an investigation has been made it has been proven that the packer does not get enough money to cover the loss.
That is purely a matter of fact, of course.

If that is the position, then I assume the packers would be just as anxious as anybody else to have some other arrangement. However my officials inform me that on each occasion the matter has been checked it has been found that the amount of money taken in has not entirely covered the loss sustained.

I believe reference has been made to Bang's disease during the discussion on these items. Have the minister and his department given serious consideration to this difficulty with which cattle raisers are confronted? It affects beef herds as well as dairy herds. It is estimated by the federal Department of Agriculture in Washington that the cattle raisers of the United States suffered a loss of between $50,000,000 and $60,000,000 through the inroads of Bang's disease in their herds in 1942. It seems to me that there are two. definite factors in connection with this incurable disease with which cattle are afflicted. First there is the effect on humans through the consumption of milk not pasteurized, produced by cattle with Bang's disease, and second there is the terrific loss occasioned by this disease which must be
borne by the farmers. I submit, Mr. Chairman, and I have some knowledge of the importance of this matter, that Bang's disease as it affects the cattle industry is even more important on the one hand, and more dangerous on the other, than even tuberculosis in cattle. I would strongly recommend to the minister and his departmental heads that a sum of money be set aside in the estimates for the control and study of Bang's disease in cattle, and that veterinary inspectors be employed' throughout Canada to investigate this disease and if possible recommend to cattle raisers the precautions that may be taken in order to curtail its inroads.
Bang's disease is not only one of the most insidious diseases with which cattle may be infected, but it is also one of the most easily transmitted diseases. A cat moving from one barn to another may transmit Bang's disease from an infected herd to a herd that is clean, or a truck from the stockyard going into a farmer's yard will carry the infection of Bang's disease into an otherwise clean herd. Up to the present time there has been only one control of Bang's disease, and that is the slaughtering of the cattle. Whether it be a pure-forcd dairy herd, a highly priced herd, or just the ordinary herd, the only way in which to eliminate the disease in that herd is to have the herd slaughtered, and then to have a very thorough cleaning of the bams and the barnyard and also of the pasture fields where the infection of this disease lingers. In Great Britain, where they have a milder climate, one of the first questions asked by an intending .purchaser of a farm is, " Has there been Bang's disease on this farm?" Because the infection carries over into the pasture fields as well as from one barn or one barnyard to another.
This disease is important because of the terrific loss it occasions to the farmer, and because of the danger to human life, to consumers particularly of unpasteurized milk. I am given to understand, and I believe this is correct, that many pure-bred herds of cattle are infected with Bangs' disease. No restrictions or control under the Department of Agriculture are exercised through the health of animals branch with respect to an animal being sold from one herd into another. There is no obligation, except that of integrity and fairness, upon a cattle owner to advise a purchaser of cattle that his herd is infected with Bang's disease. The result is, and I think I am correct in saying this, that at least fifty per cent of the herds in Ontario are infected with Bang's disease.
Supply-Agriculture
That is a serious statement, if it is true.

My experience in the three years since I have made a study of this disease is that at least in the territory with which I am familiar approximately fifty per cent of the herds are infected with Bang's disease. That may or may not be known to the cattle raisers because it is an insidious disease and it may have been present with a herd for several years before the owner of the herd becomes aware of it.
May I say this in reference to the statement made by the minister. Where the milk is pasteurized the danger of humans contracting undulamt fever is eliminated because the germ from Bang's disease is killed by the pasteurization. The germ, however, not only affects humans through the consumption of unpasteurized milk, but affects also the breeding and the crop of calves from one year to another. A cattle raiser will lose perhaps one, two and sometimes three years in the breeding of his Stock through the infection of Bang's disease.

To say nothing of the
flow of milk.

Quite so. He loses his milk production as well as his cows. Two of the leading dairymen in Ontario were talking to me just a few weeks ago about Bang's disease. I could put their names on the record if that were desired. One of them in particular, the owner of one of the most highly-prized jersey herds in Ontario, told me that he had fought this disease for ten years and ultimately slaughtered his herd. He also stated that in view of what he had learned as he went along he would have been better off if he had slaughtered his herd ten years ago and started all over again.
I am glad that this matter has been mentioned in the house by the hon. member for New Westminster. The matter has also been brought up in the past from the point of view of the health of human beings by the hon. member for Renfrew South. Time and again the subject has been brought up in this house, and it seems to me that from the point of view of cattle raisers in Canada the minister would be well advised not only to have his officials give more attention to the study of Bang's disease, but also to provide a sum of money in his estimates that would make it possible to have a veterinary inspection of all our herds, particularly in eastern Canada. I say eastern Canada for this reason, that it has been found that Bang's disease is an in-
side disease. As a matter of fact, only one and a half to two per cent of the cattle exported from our prairie provinces and from the plains of the United States in 1942 and 1943 were infected with Bang's disease. Apparently, from the facts we have learned, Bang's disease is an inside disease. It develops much more pro-lifically in herds that are stall fed, or stall fed part of the season, and particularly it has been our experience that the disease has developed in herds that have been stabled in banked Or underground bams. I submit therefore that it is much more important to have the investigation started in Ontario than perhaps in any other part of the dominion. I trust that the minister will put a sufficient sum of money in his estimates to provide for a veterinary inspection, and let us know to begin with what percentage of the herds of Ontario are really infected with Bang's disease.
I do not wish to discuss the matter further, but it does seem to me, from my own experience and that of my neighbours and of the people with whom I have come in contact, owners of pure-bred herds and owners of the ordinary herds, that Bang's disease is one of the most devastating diseases with which our beef and dairy cattle are afflicted, I sincerely trust, as I know he will, that the minister will take full cognizance of this plague, because it is really a plague with which the cattle raisers of Canada have to contend.

I am very glad that the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, has brought this matter up again. I think every time the estimates of this particular department have been presented in the last number of years I have asked the minister what advances have been made in the treatment of this disease. What the hon. member says is undoubtedly true, that it is perhaps the most insidious and most destructive disease affecting cattle in the older settled provinces to-day; and I do not believe the hon. member's statement that fifty per cent of the herds in provinces like Ontario are affected is any too high.
At one time or another.

I know that in a great many instances when cattle have been slaughtered threre has been no compensation from the government. The presence of the disease is often concealed when it would be very much better for the man himself and for the cattle industry if it were made known.

And it is transmitted.

Supply-A griculture

It is transmitted from one herd to another through sales, and, as the hon. member says, it can be sent on a man's feet or a calf's feet from one herd to another. It destroys the efficiency of the herd. Nine times out of ten, where the disease has existed for a considerable length of time, the man has to get rid of his herd entirely, and even then he cannot be sure that he is free of the disease for a certain length of time. I understand, of course, that we have some kind of test. I believe certain discoveries have been made in the agricultural college at Guelph, whereby one can tell when a herd is free from the disease or when it has the disease. I understand that when cattle are shipped to the United States in many cases they have to undergo this blood test, and if they are found to be free of disease their entry is permitted.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of the remarks which have been made: by the hon. member for Northumberland. It is high time that the department did something to curb the disease or to make a study of it in order that it may be curbed in the near future. I do not think there is any doubt that its ravages and the losses it occasions are far greater than those suffered from tuberculosis or any other communicable disease to which cattle are subject.

There has been some check kept, of course, and some investigations made with regard to the matter. Tests are made at the laboratory at Hull, and blood is sent to that laboratory from all over Ontario. The tests which were made in 1942 showed that 1-7 of those coming in were reactors; that is, the percentage of animals for which the blood was sent in for checking amounted to only 1-7 of reactors.
Would not those very largely . be from cattle which were destined for shipment to the United States?

I assume they would be, and I was just going to give some other figures. We have some Bang's disease statistics which I think, in view of some of the statements made, should be put on the record. They are brought up to January 25, 1944. Total herds under test in Canada, 2,660. By provinces: Prince Edward Island, 8; Nova Scotia, 300: New Brunswick, 9; Quebec, 192; Ontario, 2,105; Manitoba, 4; Saskatchewan, 18; Alberta, 7; British Columbia, 17. Of those herds, 1,776 are those which are now called listed herds, that is they are free of Bang's disease. For Ontario the figures are
1,559 out of 2,105. The number of cattle represented in that check is 74,763 head, of which 58,940 were in Ontario. The average number of animals in a herd was 28. The percentage of infection in cattle was 2-8, and in the herds 16 per cent; that is 16 per cent of the herds had reactors, infected animals, in them. Infected herds clear after first test, 62 per cent, after second test 15 per cent, after third and subsequent tests 23 per cent. Time required to complete the report tests at research station, three to four days. That is the record of the checks up to date.

In the light of the figures which the minister has just submitted I would like to make this comment. I assume figures have been compiled from the different tests which have been made, but actual experiences proves this. First, the minister has given the percentage of cattle in a herd which have been infected.
No, the percentage of herds that have infected cattle in them.

I submit that even that does not give the true picture, and I suggest this to the minister. If one cow in a stable has . Bang's disease, and there are 25 head in that stable, you can figure that within twelve or fifteen months twenty cattle will have it, because it is a most contagious disease. While the minister's figures are enlightening as statistics, they not only do not give the true picture but certainly Should not be submitted to minimize the conditions.
No; they are submitted to give the facts. The hon. member said, fifty per cent of the herds are infected; this shows 16 per cent only of those checked, and 84 per cent have none.

Those figures were taken as the minister submitted them, but I repeat, and it is an astounding fact, that when you bring to light the herds which are infected, herds which were infected say in 1939 and have grown out of it as far as the actual effect on the breeding of stock is concerned, still remain carriers and can infect any herd directly or indirectly. These figures in themselves do not reflect the practical effect of the infection in herds.
Another thing: as the minister has said, the department has carried on experiments in the station at Hull in connection with the inoculation of calves. All that is in an experimental stage, and my experience with the department has been that not enough attention has been given to it, not enough money

has been spent to be effective and in order that the departmental officials can advise cattle-raisers what they should do.
As I said a minute ago, there is nothing certain about inoculation. It has been tried in calves from four to six, four to eight and four to ten months. With the new serum which I believe the department has developed, they are advising the inoculation of heifers or animals up to twenty-four months and thirty months. In New York state, I believe the minister will agree with me, they have adopted the policy of inoculation of cattle- not only their calves and heifers but their breeding stock. I think that policy has been adopted within the last twelve months, but the import of the whole thing is that we should recognize the devastation that is being caused, the terrific monetary loss, the national loss of food as well as the menace to human beings. In my opinion the investigation of Bang's disease is the most important item in this connection. It is causing greater loss of time and production and greater monetary loss than infection from tuberculosis or any other disease.
I do not wish to magnify the difficulties nor do I wish to paint too dark a picture, but I am afraid the statistics the minister has given-

By way of correction, I did not read the statistics to prove anything except that fifty per cent is a high figure. I do not want anyone to suggest that I am not just as anxious to eradicate Bang's disease as any other member who is speaking here.

I would not suggest that for a moment. Perhaps the figure which the hon. member for Northumberland and I quoted is too high. On the other hand, the minister did quote statistics, and I do not think they give a true picture, because I fear that a great many of the herds that were worst affected did not appear in it. There seems to be an inclination, on the part of a man who has a herd in which there is Bang's disease to keep it quiet and try to work at it himself.
Most of the' herds I have taken in have been put under the supervision of the department to clean them up.

May I offer a suggestion? If the minister wrants a true picture there are certain counties, I understand, where they are testing herds for tuberculosis to bring them under the restricted areas plan. Would it be too difficult at the same time
You cannot do them ac the same time.

Then you might do them when you came back. At any rate, it would be a good thing if some area were gone over, such as a county for tuberculosis, going into everyone's herd and finding out how many there are.

The main reason we are not doing that is that the facts are as they have been brought out in connection with tuberculosis. We have not enough men now to do the work. The chief reason for not doing what is being suggested is that we have not the man-power at the moment to do it and have not had for some time. We are cleaning up tuberculosis, and one difficulty is that you cannot do the two operations at the same time. You have to double up on the work.
Could you not make the blood test at the same time?

I understand not.
Mr. FRASER (Northumberland)!: I submit that the blood test could be taken at the same time for both diseases.

Bang's disease or contagious abortion in cattle is a vital problem that cannot be too strongly impressed upon the people. In the years I have sat in the house, time after time, this question has come up. In our own dairy herd at home years ago we had a plague of Bang's disease and I think I know personally something of what has been described this afternoon by the hon. member for Northumberland, so far as its effects are concerned. It is one of the most dangerous and damaging of all diseases among cattle, not only from the standpoint of loss of production and of calves but also from the resulting scourge of undulant fever, which is induced among human beings by drinking milk of that type. In connection with tests for Bang's disease, as the minister knows, the blood tests are taken and are then sent to the animal diseases research institute in Hull, Quebec. As the hon. member for Haldimand has said, there are also facilities at Guelph agricultural college for tests in connection with Bang's disease, and if I remember rightly in the laboratories at Queen's park facilities are also provided for that purpose. I do not normally cite individual instances, and I do not do so on this occasion except by way of illustrating a situation. But here is the situation that exists, and it is one that should

Supply-Agriculture
come before the committee. I have brought it to the minister's attention before and I do not want him to think that in bringing it up again here my object is unduly to embarrass him.
In one particular herd, that of Mr. Greenwood, at Woodbridge, which is not far from my own home, three tests were made for Bang's disease. This gentleman has an excellent herd of cattle, pure bred, registered and accredited. These tests were all negative, but a fourth test was made in which one cow showed positive. Shortly after that a test of this cow was made at Guelph agricultural college and perhaps at some other place, although I am not sure about that. At any rate, it was made and showed negative. Of course the herd as a whole was then incapable of being listed as Bang's-disease free. Mr. Greenwood's contention was that' at the animal research institute in Hull some error may have been made in the testing. That may or may not be so, but in his mind that was a possibility. Because of the fact that there was a conflict between the tests, the department still holds that in that particular instance the positive test must be the one that governs., I understand from the department that sometimes these tests show at one time positive and at another time negative, but it is hard for the breeder to understand this if the tests are properly made.

It is
generally negative and then positive.
I had no object in giving precedence to one over the other.

But it is
generally that way.

In any event, in this particular instance I know that four cattle were sold out of the herd and allowed by the department to go into other herds which were already listed, although this herd had never been listed owing to the fact that it had not had a negative reaction in each instance. I bring this to the minister's attention again, not because I wish to be merely critical, but because these are things which it is very difficult for the minister or the department or members of parliament to explain to breeders. Here is a single cow in the whole herd showing a positive reaction just once in all these tests and because of that the herd cannot get certification. I suggest to the minister that that instance may be illustrative of others. It may look like going pretty far, and it is a situation which would easily work a good deal of hardship and inconvenience to a bona fide breeder who is attempting to maintain a herd which is a credit to himself and of great assistance to production. I cite this case merely to seek some relief and as an illustration in the hope that the experience gained from it may be utilized to advantage by other breeders who from time to time have like problems.

This question has been brought up on several occasions, particularly by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. I brought it up a couple of years ago, and I am not sure that we are making the necessary headway with it. I think it is realized that prevention is better and cheaper than cure.
I have an item here which may be of interest. It was taken from the Western Producer of March 9 of this year. It is headed:	"Hopeful of Controlling Bang's
Through Vaccine," and reads as follows:
Two Alberta cattlemen, Dean W. L. Carlyle of Calgary, and Sam Henderson of Lacombe, returned recently from a conference on Bang's disease control, held at Denver, Colorado. They represented Alberta cattle associations, and carried instructions to learn the new methods being tried out in the United States for control of this disease.
The men stated that 97-4 per cent of the pure bred cattle breeders in Colorado were practising calfhood vaccination to control the disease, and that of 500,000 head vaccinated in the last three years, only seven later developed Bang's.
"They are only in the experimental stage, but the outlook for controlling this disease is distinctly hopeful," said Dean Carlyle on his return. "I hope we can get cooperative action of the same kind in Canada."
We have followed the lead of the United States in several other matters, and if they are able to give us a lead in this I do not think we should be slow in following it. I also believe we should not be slow in following some new cures that have been suggested in Canada. If some of the old ones do not give the results then it would be wise to start out on something new. During the year 1943 how many cattle were slaughtered in Canada because of Bang's disease? What amount was paid as compensation by the government, and what is the loss to the owners of the cattle that were slaughtered? I ask these questions because when we get the destruction in dollars and cents it sometimes impresses itself on our minds more than anything else.

That is exactly the
question raised by the hon. member for Northumberland. He has suggested that we ought to be doing the same thing for Bang's disease as we are doing for tuberculosis. As a matter of fact we are not. We are not paying for cattle slaughtered on account of Bang's disease. We do not control their slaughter or pay for
Supply-Agriculture

their slaughter. He suggested that we should be doing that the same as we are for tuberculosis. In most of the states they are paying for the slaughter of cattle that have Bang's disease, the same as we do for tuberculosis. They may not be paying for them on the same basis, but they are paying for them. The question has been raised, and what I have said with regard to it is that our main difficulty at the moment is man-power with which to handle it. We are facing a difficult problem now with tuberculosis and our men are more than fully employed with that. We are not able to get along with it as rapidly as we would like to. We figure it would take at least fifty additional men to do the work that we think we ought to be doing now. Our main difficulty is to get more men to handle this problem along with the problem we are dealing with.

I take it that as soon as men
are available something drastic will be done to curtail this disease.

Even with the information we have we are not able to enter upon a plan at the moment such as we have for tuberculosis. A great many farmers are very careful about it themselves. Most of the breeders will not admit animals to their farms until they have been tested. Farmers shipping cattle from one part of Canada to another insist upon tests being made. When we bought the cattle in the west in 1937 as a result of the drought, all the female cattle that passed through the pasture at Carberry were tested for Bang's disease and tuberculosis. We have a complete record of those cattle. They were not the best of the cattle, and I would think that their record would probably be as high, at least as high, as it would be for the general cattle population over that area. The actual number of reactors was very low. We have been making checks wherever it is possible to make them, and we have been making them as fully as we can with the staffs available. But we have not undertaken to pay for the slaughter of cattle on account of Bang's disease as we have on account of tuberculosis.
Would the minister give the percentage for Alberta as he did for Ontario?

I did not give the percentage for Ontario; I gave the percentage for all Canada. I hesitate to give the percentage for the different provinces, for this reason. In Manitoba there were only seven herds tested. I would take it from the figure here that the person who asked to have the test made knew that there was some Bang's in the herd, because the percentage is very high. Alberta

only had twelve. I would assume the same thing with regard to Alberta. The percentage is very high there; but when you take the percentage from Prince Edward Island across the country of all the cattle the average percentage is 2-7. I think it would give a wrong impression to put out the figure for Alberta and Manitoba, because it is unreasonably high.

The minister said that he thought the breeders knew there was Bang's in their herds when they asked to have them tested. I think that is the wrong inference to draw. I am inclined to think that the opposite is the fact; that certain herds had been tested locally before they were submitted to the department for certification, and that little if any Bang's disease had shown up.

It would depend entirely on the individual. I recall the first year I was here the question came up as to whether we were going to mark animals that, were positive. I had a strong representation from the cattle breeders objecting to marking them. Hon. members who were here at the time will recall that we had intended to put a big "B" on their cheek so that any one walking into the stable could see that the animal had been tested and was positive for Bang's disease. There was objection to that, and we finally put the "B" in the ear of the animal. We had objection from the breeders and others who said that if a man walks into our barns and sees a big "B" on the animal we will not be able to sell anything.
You are using the ear now?

At the present time we are marking them in the ear with a "B", and anyone who wishes to look over the animals can see that they have been tested and that certain ones have reacted positively for Bang's. The marking is there. That was the question at that time. It has come along from there to where it is at the present time, that nobody questions the marking, and we have an agitation in this house for having them all tested. I think every one would be tested if we had enough men and enough money to go out and test all the herds in the country. With regard to assisting in killing the animals by paying for their slaughter, I am informed by the officials that if we were to undertake to do that, the statement made by the hon. member for Haldimand and the hon. member for Northumberland would be borne out. At least we think the result would be that more animals would be slaughtered for Bang's disease than are now

slaughtered for tuberculosis. That emphasizes the problem that will have to be dealt with as soon as we can get the necessary man-power.

I should like to revert to
the matter referred to by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit me to ask one further question in connection with Bang's disease. Has the minister had any complaints in regard to errors in testing at the Hull laboratories?

I should have dealt
with that point when I was speaking. I would not say it is a common thing, but it does sometimes happen that an animal gives a positive result at one time and a negative result at another, and may continue to do' so. You may check that animal one day and get a negative result; another time the result will be positive. I think I am correct in saying that in some cases after a very considerable number of tests they have agreed that probably the animal will continue negative. However, if we are to apply the principle that once an animal tests positive something must be done about it, I do not see how we can pass up any animal that once gives a positive result. I am told, too, though I do not fully understand these matters as I am sure most hon. members do not understand them, that when the blood of these animals is sent in for test there is the possibility of doubt in some cases. A person who is very strict may say that the result is positive; another person may consider it doubtful, and perhaps someone else would even say it was negative, though I am not sure of that. In any case there might be at least two opinions on the case. I understand there have been instances where blood of the same animal has been sent to two places, with slightly different reports from each. However, every care is taken to avoid anything of that kind by having all cases dealt with in exactly the same way at all the stations. If the blood is sent to two official stations, th'e report from each should be the same, though of course the personal element enters into all these things to a degree. Where there was doubt about an animal the only way to clear up that herd and make absolutely certain of it would be to kill or get rid of the animal. That would put the herd back in position, and that is the argument for the government paying part, of the loss. A farmer would be more likely to get rid of such an animal immediately with the government paying part.of the loss than he would be if nothing were paid.	1
If I understand the minister correctly, it is possible that where there has been only one positive reaction followed by a number of negative results, the animal might be declared free of disease.

I understand that once it is definitely classed as positive the department does not retest it. If there is any doubt about it, however; if it is a borderline case and the individual concerned expresses doubt, it may be retested.

It seems to me that is
pretty arbitrary.

I
think this question has been covered pretty well, but it seemed to me the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, put the percenr tage rather high when he said fifty per cent of the herds were infected. As a matter of fact I believe that seventy-five per cent of the cattle in Ontario, either beef cattle or dairy cattle, belong to herds tested and free from Bang's disease and tuberculosis. I doubt very much if a man would buy one of these better breeders and put it in with his herd unless it had been tested for both tuberculosis and Bang's disease. I also doubt whether a man could sell one of the better breeders in the United States, even if it came from an area free from tuberculosis, without an individual test being made. The unfortunate thing is that these tests are not one hundred per cent accurate, that an animal may test positive one time and negative another. That is true in connection with tuberculosis; some of the most advanced cases gave a negative result when the blood was tested, so that these tests are not absolutely conclusive. Many of the herds which become infected with Bang's disease build up their own immunities within a short time. Those cattle may go on and be fairly successful herds of breeders, but they will be carriers and in most cases will react to the blood test. It seems to me one of the things to which the department should give a great deal of attention is the inoculation of cattle with the serum used for protection against Bang's disease. My information is that if cattle are inoculated at a certain stage, perhaps before they are twelve or fifteen months old, they are made practically immune to the ravages of Bang's disease. If that is true it would seem to be the logical way to eliminate this disease.

Coming back to the matter of condemnation insurance, the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough was not quite sure of his figures. On two previous occasions I

Over what period?

That is only for one year, 1943. In that year we paid the packing companies of Canada over $500,000 more than was required to carry the condemnation insurance. When I spoke previously I appealed to the minister to have this matter handled by the government in order that we might have some control over it. On the last occasion this matter was discussed the minister told, me that payment of this condemnation insurance was not compulsory. That is correct; I can go to the packer with my live stock and say I do not want him to take off that insurance. He will reply, "Well, you can take your stock somewhere else." That is the position; it is not compulsory, but you cannot sell your stock unless you agree to this deduction. To-day that condemnation insurance takes care of other things than loss through tuberculosis, though on the statement the reason given is for tuberculosis insurance. When I ship my cattle or hogs by common carrier the law of the land requires that they have insurance to take care of them. From the moment the animal enters the truck or the railway car until it comes out again, I have to pay for insurance to cover it. But when you have a cow spread on the killing floor, or a cow breaking its leg on the killing floor, surely that is not the responsibility of the farmer. Yet he is paying for it through condemnation insurance.
I do not wish to dwell on the point; the minister knows my views in the matter. I should like to see it handled by his department or by a board of live stock commissioners. I went back in the records as far as I could trace, to 1906 and 1907, and never in any one year did it take more than half of one per cent to carry that condemnation insurance. And in forty years, a few thousand dollars each year would have been a very handy sum to be used by breeders' associations in their

efforts to get better bulls, or better sires of one kind or another. Some might say that it was too small an amount to divide among the farmers, but there were many things for which it could have been used.
While I am on my feet may I touch upon compensation for animal slaughtering? I understand this involves T.B. insurance; is that correct? We have heard about T.B. insurance, and T.B. free areas. Condemnation insurance was begun away back in 1906. because many tubercular cattle were reaching the plants. The Department of Agriculture in those early days-I do not know how early-established T.B. free areas. Those T.B. free areas were established through a two-thirds vote, and when they came in all herds were tested. Retests were made within sixty days and in every twelve months following. In that way T.B. free areas were established. At that time the rate set was two-thirds of the value of the animal. That rate was all right when one could buy a cow for $60 or $70, and received $38 for the condemned animal. That amount was placed on the purchase price of another animal. I come from an area which is to-day established as a T.B. free area, and on a cow condemned for T.B. one receives $38, or the same amount to-day as he did ten or twenty yearn ago. Yet to-day one must pay about $200 to replace the animal. The minister will realize just how unfair that is.

I raised the question myself six or seven years ago, when cows were worth about $20 a head. However at that time we continued to pay on the same basis. I doubt very much if it would be advisable to go up and down, or to follow values at all times.
That would have been a good time to eradicate tuberculosis, would it not?

I am pleased that the minister is interested in this matter, and I am sure he will see at once the injustice of the present practice. No man will ever turn down the offer of cleaning up his herd, to see that there is no T.B. in it; yet he will receive only $38 for an animal worth anywhere from $175 to $200.
In the fall of 1942 in the Red River valley we put a thousand cows into the packing plant for T.B. Look at the loss we took on those cows. If too small an amount is paid it will act as a hindrance to the eradication of T.B. I would ask the minister to give me the assurance that I could go back to Selkirk and tell the people there that he is sympathetic, and that he is going to try to do something. It is most unfair to pay only $38 for

Supply-Agriculture
an animal which within a few weeks must be replaced in the herd at about $175. It is out of all reason. The test is still being carried on, and it would appear that the department does not intend to pay any more in future, because the amount appearing in the estimates is even smaller than it has been.

What we pay is not necessarily all that the farmer receives for the animal. The regulation is that on cattle we pay 66f per cent of the value of the animal, with a limitation of $60 on the value of grades. This means that we might pay $40. On purebred cattle we pay two-thirds, with a limitation of $150 on the value. That means we may pay $100. But in addition to that, the fact that an animal is condemned does not mean that the farmer cannot sell it. He may send the animal to the abattoir, and it will be paid for on some basis. It may be paid for only as tankage. That would be so if none of the animal is fit for human consumption. It may be paid for on the basis of cutting out a small gland in the neck. That may be the only part of the animal which shows contamination. All the rest of the animal would be paid for. That is, a farmer may receive almost full value for the cow as a meat animal. The simple statement, therefore, that the farmer gets only what the government pays, is scarcely in accordance with the facts. For example, to give an exact case, I know of one animal which within the last two years reached the market after being condemned for tuberculosis. The person who sold that animal got over $100 for it. In that instance, while upon inspection the animal reacted for TB., there was only a small gland in the neck which was affected, and that was the only part which had to be destroyed. So on that basis the figures given by the hon. member do not cover the whole returns.
Reference has been made to what is sometimes called tuberculosis contamination in hogs. Perhaps the highest figure in the whole list of things for which hogs are condemned comes opposite tuberculosis. But the list covers a page and a half of different things for which hogs may be condemned.
Yes, but -19 of one per cent covers all the others.

One of the bigger groups is contamination. In connection with swine there were 122,865, only portions of which were contaminated. Coming to tuberculosis, we find that 4,726 carcasses were condemned but the number of carcasses of which only portions were condemned was 2,684,386.
You cannot just take the value of the hogs that come in and then take the condemnation figure, and then say that you have a comparison there from which you can draw conclusions. It would not be possible to do that. That is why those who are asking for some change in policy or that some report be made from time to time suggest that there ought to be an investigation made. That is why investigations have been made from time to time. If you just say that so many hogs came on to the market; that so many hogs were destroyed because they were condemned, and that one half of one per cent of the value of the hogs is taken by the packing plants, one could arrive at the conclusion that the packing plants were getting too much. But you cannot do it in that way, and I am afraid that that is what the hon. member was doing.
I am not saying that the packers are not getting more than they are entitled to, because I have no reason for saying one thing more than another. I am simply saying that any investigations which have been made have tended to indicate that the fund just about covers the amount.

I agree in the main with what the minister has said. But take a hog that has a little T.B. in the neck. There is half of one per cent collected for that. The farmer gets the full price for his hog but the packer sells the full hog.
I understand that that is all considered when the investigations are made. They take into consideration what the packer got for his hogs and what he paid out.
I have taken these things into consideration too. Talk about making a T.B. free area; I have gone through all that. You do get the odd cow which makes beef but they are very few and far between.
It is really the other way around.

I was accused of sitting on boards around Winnipeg, but if you had said that I had been in the packing plant, as 1 have been, finding out things, you would have been nearer the point. When we had that TB. free area I followed the cattle through the packing plant. When an animal goes into the tank you get only the hide, you have to pay for the killing, and you would think these fellows were carpenters the way they charge you for killing an animal.

I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Selkirk says about the condemnation insurance being too high, but he is entirely wrong when he says that it is

compulsory. It is not compulsory. I know a great many shippers who have never paid condemnation insurance. If you sell your stock outright to the drover the drover takes the responsibility, but if you ship your stock on a commission basis you are perfectly free to designate whether you want to pay condemnation insurance or not.
I should like to say a word in regard to the treatment we have received from the department with respect to T.B. tested animals. Some years ago I had my herd of pure-bred cattle subjected to the test. I had eleven reactors. I considered them worth about $6,000 and I received in the final analysis a little over $200 apiece for these animals. That does not sound very much like the $38 that my hon. friend spoke about a few minutes ago.
Were the hon. member's cattle pure-bred Aberdeen Angus?
Yes.
I am just a poor man, mine were grades.

I should like to point this out, that of the eleven head, only one went to the tank. All the rest were slaughtered and the meat was used for domestic purposes. I am inclined to think my hon. friend has overdrawn the picture considerably. I spent a day in his district just two and a half weeks ago and I saw a very nice herd of dairy cattle, Holsteins. The owner of this herd was talking about selling them. I asked him what he thought his herd was worth and he said, "I would be glad if I could get $125 apiece." He had some lovely cows. Again that does not sound very much like the $175 or $200 that the hon. member was speaking of. I am inclined to think some of our hon. friends in the C.C.F. would make a little more progress if they were not quite so extravagant, in their statements. They seem to think that they must overdraw the picture all the time; that they must stretch their imaginations in presenting a case. Some of us are not impressed by these extravagant statements. I believe that we can make a little better progress if we keep our feet on the ground and just be a little conservative in the statements we make.
It is always well to be conservative.' .

I agree with my hon. friend, but I am surprised that he has not had more influence upon hon. gentlemen of the C.C.F. They do cooperate with his party at times, 
but he does not seem to have influenced them in presenting a more reasonable case before the house.

I would draw to the attention of my hon. friend the member for Dauphin, when he talks about misquoting, that last night he said that he quoted me from Hansard, which was an untruthful statement. He said that I took 280 days to put 300 pounds on a steer. The way I felt when he was speaking was, "where ignorance is bliss "tis folly to be wise," and I held my tongue, but I am correcting him now. I said, and it will be found in Hansard, that I would take 180 days to put 300 pounds on the back of a steer, and you have to be a good feeder to do it-irrespective of what you do yith your Aberdeen Angus. So do not talk about overdrawing the picture.

I thought, Mr. Chairman, we were discussing this item in a non-political manner, but the discussion seems to be getting a little out of hand. I do not wish to prolong it. I just want to say to the hon. member for Selkirk that when he first started to speak he quoted the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough as having been mixed up in his figures. The hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough was giving the figures for Ontario, and I think the figures were secured from the hog breeders' association. They showed an average collected of $250,000 a year and only about 3.000 head condemned which would bring it to about $75,000. That leaves a large balance running from $175,000 to $200,000. We must remember that fully 15 to 20 per cent of all the parts condemned are recoverable in by-products by the abattoir. To me this seems to be the only class of insurance for which no accounting has to be given, and I should like to hear a word from the minister on that.
While awaiting the minister's answer-
An answer to what?

The bon. member for Hastings South wanted the minister to clear up some point. We have had a long discussion of contagious diseases of one kind or another. The discussion has been very interesting and I think it might be of some benefit to the live stock industry.
There is another disease which is quite rampant in the province of Ontario, and possibly in the west, known as shipping fever or hemorrhagic septicaemia. The ravages of that disease are quite apparent. We in Ontario buy a: lot of cattle for feeding purposes, and hardly ever a carload comes

Supply*-Agriculture
into the neighbourhood but has to be immediately looked after or some are lost through this disease of hemorrhagic septicaemia. I have no doubt whatever that the department is aware of this disease and knows what is going on, and I should like the minister to make a short statement as to what is being done by the department to overcome the disease.

The department of course is aware of the disease and has been keeping in as close touch as possible with it from time to time. The organism producing this disease is widely distributed through nature and only becomes pathogenic through exciting influences. Serious losses occur in shipments owing to shipping poorly fed, weakened animals. Losses could be prevented if only animals with normal resistance to disease were shipped and given adequate rest and feeding en route. Vaccination is harmful unless practised a week or ten days before cattle leave the farm. Serum is of value after a movement but it is too expensive to be used in that way. This disease may affect all domestic animals including poultry. It is a disease of the soil and the germs are not normally disease-producing. It is not a suitable disease to include with those for which this act provides compulsory notice and action. The germs are always present in the soil of stockyards and places where live stock are or have been handled. Then I understand that the idea of the Canadian national live stock records is to

maintain records of all pure-bred live stock in Canada; I believe they keep all the records with the exception of those kept by the Holstein-Friesian association, including the records of the horse breeders. There is one regulation which, I believe, has irritated the horse breeders. The horse breeders are obliged to register their horses with the New York Jockey Club. Not only do they have to register in the Canadian national live stock records, but also must register with the New York Jockey Club. Then, if they are going to race their horses they are compelled to register with the Incorporated Racing Association. That seems to be a rather elaborate procedure to go through.
I am not objecting so much to that, if that is considered necessary by the racing associations. What I am objecting to is that horses should be allowed to come from the United States and race on our tracks in Canada, when they do not have to register in the Canadian national live stock records. It seems to me that if our breeders are obliged to register in New York state there should be a reciprocal arrangement whereby they are forced to register in Canada, if they wish to race their horses here.
The difficulty is that the race-horse breeders in Canada find that there is a lack of scrutiny with respect of horses coming to this country. Unless we have some check on them by way of registration we can have no indication as to whether they are registered, even under the New York Jockey Club regulations. The result is that, to use a slang expression, ringers are put on the race tracks, and our breeders must compete against these unscrupulous methods of doing business. Unfortunately we are not giving enough attention to the matter, or protecting our own breeders.
To my mind it is important that we assert ourselves, and that we give the necessary protection to our breeders. True, I will admit that the breeding of race-horses has not become extensive; but it is a hobby enjoyed by certain men. They like to breed that type of live stock. My purpose in raising the question is to point out that, after all, in the main, horse-racing is supposed to be a rich man's game. Fortunately, there are some honest-to-goodness dirt farmers who still like to breed fast race-horses, and I do not think they should be discouraged. It is on their behalf I am speaking, because if one were to go through the records of all types of live stock breeding, and particularly in Canada, he would find that the finest, the very best live stock is produced by the honest-to-goodness dirt farmer.

True, we welcome the wealthy man who enters the game as a hobby. They have been able to make their contribution by bringing together certain families of animals, and producing good results.
