Let me tell the committee that there is something in the quality of a man's mind that finds its expression in the proper mating together of animals, to bring about certain desired results.
I have in mind a man who happened to be a neighbour of mine, and liked to breed fancy race-horses. At one time he had an opportunity to purchase a sire for the sum of S50. A wealthy man had paid 850,000 for the same sire, but did not use him or mate him with the proper mares to get results. But because this dirt farmer understood the particular virtues of that stallion, and could analyse his qualities and mate him with the proper females, in a few years he was in a position to produce one of the best and greatest money-making race-horses on the Canadian circuit. Then he found out that because he was making so much money the stewards of the Canadian racing association * found some excuse to put him off the tracks.
I am not blaming the federal department for that because, after all, the racing association is under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. But I do point out that that is a matter which should be looked into as early as possible, and that the racing association should be under the control of a commission. There should be far more jurisdiction over it than there is at the present time.
The whole thing follows out a certain scheme and philosophy. I feel that I am here to protect the interests of the honest-to-goodness dirt farmer. If it were not out of order I should like at this point to analyse some of the results of breeding, as they are set out in the national live stock records. I could show from those records that the greatest cows in Canada to-day were the result of careful mating under the control of honest-to-goodness dirt farmers. If one will analyse the records of performance as they are set out in the Dairy Journal he would find that while some wealthy people own cattle which they milk four times a day, and produce certain records, the average farmer who cannot afford to milk four times a day obtains very good results. As one goes down the list he will find that it is the honest-to-goodness dirt farmer, the farmer who has the cows which milk only twice a day, who has the better record. His record is even better than those fellows who milk four times a day.
I see the hon. member for Haldimand smiling. Well, he has a neighbour in his constituency, an honest-to-goodness dirt farmer, who produced the first 30,000-pound cow in Canada. That was Jemima of Riverside. I could give the committee the history of many other cows, such as Paulina Calantha Posch, whose progeny were the foundation of many Holstein herds to-day. The same blood was the foundation of that great farm, Hudson Heights, owned by Mr. T. B. Macaulay, who sold some of these high-priced cows. Paulina Calantha Posch was a cow bred by an ordinary dirt fanner in my own county, which I have the honour to represent.
Then there were other sires like Prince Calanthus Abberkerk, which was owned by an Oxford county farmer. Those were some of the greatest animals on record in Canada, and were selections made by honest-to-goodness dirt farmers.
We cannot afford to neglect some of these things which give encouragement to ordinary farmers. I am quite prepared to admit that the raising of race-horses is a game for the rich man. There are very few ordinary farmers who can afford to take the risk of going into that line of business. There is one increase, which is largely due to a new appointment, that of agricultural commissioner. That is the only addition to the staff. What are the duties of the commissioner?

The commissioner is Mr. J. G. Robertson. It will be remembered that a few years ago we appointed an agricultural commissioner, who was sent to London. Unfortunately he lost his life in the sinking of a ship in 1940 or 1941, and the vacancy was not filled until this last year. Mr. Robertson is now in London.

I should like to know what work the marketing service carries on at the present time. We have two marketing services, one under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the other under the ' Department of Agriculture. What work is the latter carrying on?

The marketing service of this department was set up as a new service in 1936, the year that I took over the department. Prior to that the department was organized into branches associated with different farm products. In 1936 we organized the department into four divisions, as they are indicated in these estimates; science service, production service, marketing service,

and special. The terms used to designate these services indicate pretty well what they are. Under science service, scientific investigations are carried on into farming, and the experimental farms sendee then tries to carry out some of the suggestions made. The production service is concerned with promoting production of the best kinds of farm products, and the marketing service is interested in the marketing of these products. Under marketing service we find such items as agricultural economics, dairy products, subsidies for cold storage warehouses, fruits and vegetable products, live stock and live stock products, and the marketing of agricultural products generally.
Our chief objective in setting up the marketing service was to give first emphasis to the necessity of finding markets for farm products. As the hon. member has stated, there is a service in the Department of Trade and Commerce which attempts to take care of marketing generally, but it was thought at that time, and experience has proved that it was a proper thought, that special emphasis should be placed upon the necessity of finding markets for farm products. It will be recalled that from 1931 to 1935 or 1936, in fact almost down to the beginning of the war, there were piling up in Canada very considerable surpluses of farm products which we found difficulty in marketing. When we found difficulty in marketing any particular product our farmers had to go out of production of that product, and the result was that in many lines of farm production from 1934 to 1936 we were down pretty close to the bottom. We made an inquiry at that time, which was fully discussed in the house and outside. We sent a delegation to Great Britain to examine the whole marketing position in Great Britain and on the continent, and they came back and made a report. That report was not acceptable to everybody. It will be recalled that at the time it was questioned whether any further copies should be printed, and the printing was finally stopped after an almost complete distribution of the report had been made all over Canada If anybody wants to know the history of marketing I recommend ^ reading of that report, some copies of which can still be found roundabout. That report gives a true picture of the conditions that existed then in the British market and on the European continent. It gives a true picture of the marketing of farm products back over a considerable period of time.

Supply-Agriculture
The report recommended that certain things be done, and we have done many of these things, particularly since the war began. As a result we have been able to market a very much greater volume of our farm products than any of us ever had thought might have been marketed from the farms of this country. The whole experience in connection with that service from the time it was set up has indicated that we certainly need in Canada, and I think in the Department of Agriculture, an organization that is intent upon finding markets for farm products both at home and abroad, and that we should proceed to spend, not less money upon it, but more in order to make sure that these markets are found and made available to our farmers.

I think the minister is
right.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before we took recess I was saying that the minister was probably right in setting up this marketing service for the Department of Agriculture, but I do not understand why he has increased the estimate on marketing and decreased the estimate on production, at a time when there is a great demand for supplies and most agricultural products are being rationed.
I should think that now we need a larger estimate for production and a smaller estimate for marketing. No doubt we shall need an increased estimate for marketing services after the war, but at this time it looks to me as though, when the marketing service of the Department of Agriculture opens up any market, the wartime prices and trade board comes along and blocks it. When we had a market for our certified seed potatoes in the United States the export board banned the export of seed, and the result was that a large quantity of certified seed was left in Canada, especially in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, and had to be sold at a much lower price, for table stock. Some of this seed was even dumped at the end of the season. During the months of January, February and March we were refused export permits. I believe this was caused by the wartime prices and trade board, and I should like to see more cooperation between the two boards and the department. It looks to me as though in the last two years the wartime prices and trade board
has been opposing everything which the marketing branch of the Department of Agriculture has tried to do.
Mr. S'ENN: I am somewhat in agreement with the hon. member who has just spoken about this matter of marketing at this time. The minister made quite a statement at six o'clock, saying that the marketing services had been set up in their present form about 1936 or 1937, when he first came into the department. I am free to admit that they did very good work up to the time of the war. However, the minister referred to a report which is commonly known as the Shaw report and gave it credit for the increased marketing which has been experienced since that time. In my opinion any increase which has occurred in the marketing of farm products, particularly in Great Britain and other foreign parts, has been due to the war itself and its needs and not to any report which was issued prior to the war by any official of the department.
I doubt very much the necessity of having such a large marketing service at the present time, particularly when one takes into consideration the number of boards which are marketing a large part of our production. We have the wheat board marketing our wheat, the meat board marketing our meat products of all kinds, the dairy products board looking after the marketing of dairy products, the special products board concerned with the marketing of other products. Just why the minister is so anxious to keep the department at its full strength at this time is difficult to understand. 1 doubt very much the advisability of having so large a department. I think I know what the minister will say, that a number of officials who are in the marketing service here go to make up the boards which are handling these products as they are shipped to other countries. That is very true. But once more I am going to criticize these boards for having no producer representation. I believe we would get along much better and the boards would have to a much greater extent the confidence of the producers if the producers were represented upon them.
I do not intend to pursue the matter farther. The ministers may have information which I have not to support the necessity of keeping up such a large marketing service when we have so many boards organized for the purpose of marketing our products abroad, and when there is so large a demand for those products that, as the hon. member who just sat down remarked, we cannot fill the demands.

There is one point in connection with a matter which has been raised to which I think some attention should be given. It was suggested that we had this

Supply-Agriculture

marketing report back in 1936 and that the increase which has come in connection with the marketing of farm, products is largely as a result of the war. I would instance just one farm product to indicate the extent to which that is a fact. With regard to cheese, Canadian production in 1907 was 204 million pounds and our exports to Britain were 190 million pounds. Coming down to 1934, we produced 99 million pounds and exported 58 million pounds. In 1935 we produced 100 million pounds and exported 52 million pounds; that is the low point of our exports over the whole reported period. In 1936 we had these investigations made of which I spoke and started trying to encourage in the latter part of that season the production and export of cheese. By 1937 we were producing 130 million pounds and exported 80 million pounds; in 1938 we produced 123 million pounds and exported 75,950,000 pounds; in 1938 we exported 90,945,000 pounds. Before the war started we had increased our exports to Great Britain from 52 million to 90 million pounds, and I think that was largely the result of the activities which were taken at that time, not only on this side but in Britain. We put in Great Britain, the representative of the department who was spoken of earlier, when we were asked why we had voted an extra salary this year for agricultural appointments, and we gave him some staff with which to promote the sale of cheese and other farm products in Great Britain, with the results I have just indicated, before the war started. It is true that in 1942 we had got our production of cheese up to within one million pounds of what it was in 1907. The increase in production continued through the war period, until in 1942 we produced between two hundred and three million pounds and we exported between 140 million and 150 million pounds to Great Britain. We were down in 1943 as compared with 1942 and we are up again this year as compared with last year. It is most important to promote not only marketing but production, and we are doing both. We are promoting the production of cheese at present, influencing that production to some extent by our action in connection with subsidies on milk and1 other dairy products.
Bonuses.

Cheese production is going up under that system at the present time. Of course, in the earlier years there was no bonus; it was merely a matter of assuring the farmer that there was a market for the product and a certain return for it and he produced the cheese.

The
demand must have fallen off in Britain. Was there a question about the quality of our cheese?
No.

There was
some question, I believe.

A question arose toward the end of the last war with regard to our willingness to supply cheese at a price. Perhaps I should give the figures which are here before me. In 1907 we produced in Canada 204 million pounds and in that year imports into the United Kingdom from Canada amounted to 190 million pounds and imports from New Zealand to 21 million pounds. Coming to the year I mentioned, 1935, our production had gone to 100 million pounds and our exports to the United Kingdom amounted to 52 million pounds, while New Zealand's exports to the United Kingdom had risen to 197 million pounds.
What was the reason for that?

There were two or three reasons, and one of the reasons explained in the report we were discussing is this. You could go to London in 1936 and walk down the Strand; you could see on every bus, and displayed prominently on buildings the sign, "Eat New Zealand Cheese".
Sales promotion.

But there was no Canadian sign anywhere in London at that time. We inaugurated an advertising policy partly through our own department and partly by reason of the good will of the Department of Trade and Commerce, with the result that our cheese was advertised in the same way as New Zealand cheese was being displayed, and then we went on and urged our people to produce cheese in order to meet the demand being thus created.
Can the minister give figures showing the prices realized per pound for cheese at the various times he has indicated?

In 1907 the price was 13-91 cents; in 1935, 11-62 cents; in 1936, 13-44 cents; in 1937, 14-67 cents; in 1938, 15-26 cents. That is the last year for which I have prices here, but since that time they have gone up gradually, from sixteen cents the following year, until now the actual price is twenty cents which, with other premiums and other forms of assistance, is brought up to around twenty-five or twenty-six cents.

How are the extra costs accounted for? They should be in these estimates. I am referring to extra costs resulting from the war.
The cost of the dairy board is in the war expenditures.

Glancing over this estimate here, especially the details given at page 65, I have come to the conclusion that this is about one of the best paid branches the minister has under his jurisdiction. I would not object to that but for a number of reasons. First of all, consider what the hon. member for Haldimand stated a little while ago. We have in operation a number of other boards which no doubt are carrying on some of the work that this branch of the department in other years would be expected to do. But over and above that, my reason for rising at this time is that earlier in the day, when we were discussing another branch of the department, the health of animals, the minister gave us what I thought at that time was a reasonable and logical explanation of the manner in which the salaries were adjusted. Glancing over this, however, and comparing it with the health of animals branch, I find that there are some discrepancies. For instance, the director of marketing service receives $8,500, but when you turn to the health of animals branch you find that the highest figure is $4,320. It may be said that the director of marketing service is a rather more responsible person, being more or less the head of that branch. Well, drop that for the moment and take the agricultural commissioner. There the figure is $5,280, and when you look at the health of animals branch the first person in charge gets $4,320.

You should compare
them with the director of production and the director of experimental farms. The salaries are more nearly the same.

But I submit that even taking that into consideration, when we were dealing with the health of animals, it was pointed out on a number of occasions in this session that the health of animals has a bearing on the health and welfare of human beings as well. I do not see therefore why we should have one class of men underpaid, while those in another branch are receiving a fairly reasonable remuneration. Mind you, I am not complaining, or suggesting that these persons should not be receiving what they are. I am simply pointing out that we have a number of other boards that are taking away from them a certain amount of responsibility in the work in detail and still we leave others, who are to safeguard not only the health of animals but the health of our population to some extent, in an underpaid class. It does not seem fair. While I was more or less reconciled to the statement the minister made this afternoon, as to why they could not pay those in the health of animals branch more than they were receiving, after examining this item I am not quite so satisfied.

To keep the record straight, there are of course certain things that cannot be fully calculated here. I am not certain whether these items are entirely included in the salary, but take the director of experimental farms. He lives in a house on the farm, and anyone will agree that there are some advantages in having that government house available to him.
You are fortunate to have a house of any kind in Ottawa.

His remuneration is
$7,500, which is not as low as some mentioned by my hon. friend. He is comparable with the director of marketing. Then you go on to the director of production, whose salary is something over $6,000. At the top of page 62 of the estimates there appears the item: "Director of production services, $6,300". He is a new man recently appointed. He succeeded the person who was superannuated and takes on the lowest range of salary when he begins. Then over on the page we are dealing with appears this item: "Director of marketing services, $8,500." The occupant of that position is Mr. A. M. Shaw whom we induced to leave the position as dean of the agricultural college to come to Ottawa to take this position.
I am not saying that these people are getting too much.

I understand, but I wish to keep the record straight with regard to the heads of the division and with regard to the comparison which was made a few moments ago with the heads of branches in the division of marketing services. So far as the staffs are concerned I think it will be found that generally, as I said this afternoon, these salaries are arranged' by the civil service commission in a manner Which is intended to give the same value to the different positions which entail similar work.

Can the minister give any
information to the committee as to the possibility of a market for eggs in Great Britain for the future? Most of the provinces have
Supply-Agriculture

considerably increased their flocks. While it is true that most of the provinces produce more eggs and poultry than British Columbia, still the fact remains that we as a province specialize in the production of eggs. Although the grain comes to us from the prairies, nevertheless the fact remains that the climate is such tha,t the production per head of poultry is higher in British Columbia than in any other province.
Would the hon. member leave that until we come to live stock and live stock products?
It has to do with marketing.

Live stock and live
stock products includes marketing. I have not the information at the moment, but I shall have it when the item comes up.
Is this agricultural commissioner a new position; is it a new appointment on the marketing service?

Yes; it is the position that I dealt with this afternoon. It is the position which William Allen, who lost his life crossing the Atlantic in 1941, occupied. We left it vacant until this year. One of the reasons for that was that during the war and up until very recently we thought the position could be left vacant. But now as we think we are approaching the end of the war we thought it advisable to have a man in London and this man is in London.
Who is he?
Mr. J. G. Robertson.

I was surprised to hear certain members of the committee suggesting that there should be a cut in the grant for marketing service. I know that at the presenttime there is a market for most of our agricultural products, but I think we all agree it is largely due to the war. This grant should be maintained so that the markets which we now have may be retained and provision made for taking care of surpluses which we are likely to have in Canada after the war. Certainly I should not like to see this marketing service branch curtailed in any way, because we are going to need it and its service in the post-war years. However, I believe that we should have all agricultural products under the Minister of Agriculture, particularly the marketing of them. At the present time our wheat is marketed through the Department of Trade and Commerce. Has any move been made by the government to concentrate the marketing of all agricultural products in the [Mr. Reid.l
Department of Agriculture rather than in two departments, trade and commerce and agriculture, as they are at the present time?

There was a discussion with regard to that matter which spread itself, I think, over about twenty years or longer. Just at the beginning of the war the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was appointed, and I think the last time the matter was discussed here I intimated to the house that I thought two heads were probably better than one and that we would get along very well together; therefore we have not had any discussion on it since.

I was not asking for any cut in the marketing services. I was wondering why there was a cut in the production branch and an increase in the marketing services in war time. I think the marketing services should be increased, not decreased, but I think this is the wrong time to do it. In normal times I believe that seventy-five per cent of our estimates on agriculture should be spent on marketing. I believe that production will take care of itself in normal times.

I should like to be clear on the position which the Department of Trade and Commerce occupies with the Department of Agriculture in marketing problems overseas. I think it is true that this famous Shaw report did make mention of the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce over there and, to say the least, it was not flattering. Since this new agricultural commissioner has been appointed to look after marketing over in Britain to a certain extent, has the Department of Trade and Commerce a representative over there, and, if so, how is the work of the agricultural commissioner in Britain defined in relation to the work being done by the trade commissioner of the Department of Trade and Commerce?

There has been a representative of the agricultural department in London for a long time. I am not sure of the exact date but I think it was 1922. It was during the time, at any rate, that Mr. Motherwell was here as Minister of Agriculture. Shortly after he became Minister of Agriculture he appointed a representative of the Department of Agriculture to London. At a later date, I think it was when Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister, the agricultural representative was placed under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and that position remained in that relationship until Mr. Wilson passed away. In 1936 or 1937 the present position of agricultural commissioner was set up and we sent a man to Britain. One of the reasons

Supply-Agriculture
for that is that under this service all the grading is done by the marketing branch here. All the activities related to grading farm products such as cheese, butter and hogs and everything else excepting grain comes under this marketing branch.
With regard to some of the comment that was made a few moments ago may I say that the greater part of the staffs who are in the marketing branch were in some of the branches of the department before. When the branches were rearranged to constitute the divisions many of those having to do with grading were there then; they are there now. Speaking from memory, I believe six representatives of the department were in the different ports in Britain. There was one in Liverpool, one in London, one in Glasgow and so on. These persons were all placed under the direction of the commissioner who was sent over there. ' These men, located at the different ports, checked the commodities that were sent over, checked the grade and the condition of the commodity when it arrived. These men all operate now under this commissioner and have done so ever since he was sent over in 1936 or 1937. During the war, of course, that work probably has not been as important as it was before, with this exception. We are able to keep a check on the great quantities of bacon, for example, that we are sending to Britain. While there is not so much emphasis on the actual grade of the bacon going over, or even on the grade of the cheese, still we get continuous reports in that connection and try to keep our products up to standard. That is the work being done at the present time.

The hon. member for Haldi-mand asked one of the questions I intended to ask, and the minister has partly answered it. I have in my hand the report of his department, and on page 116 reference is made to the fact that Colonel Robertson was appointed as successor to Doctor William Allen. It goes on to say that Colonel Robertson's duty is to maintain close supervision and inspection of the quality and condition of Canadian agricultural products arriving in Britain. I believe the minister should give us a more detailed report in connection with Colonel Robertson. How are these goods arriving; what disposition is being made of them, and so on? Only a line or two of this report is devoted to this matter. I also have before me a report which was tabled in the house with respect to the production, export and domestic disappearance of certain agricultural products such as beef, pork, butter, cheese, eggs, apples, wheat, oats, barley and so on, and giving a comparison as
between 1939 and 1943. This table contains the reference to cheese mentioned by the minister a moment ago, showing an increase in production of 38,000,000 pounds as between those two years. It is also interesting to note that the domestic disappearance has remained fairly constant, the difference being only one per cent on the basis of the percentage of production, while exports have increased by more than 30,000,000 pounds. With respect to beef it is interesting to note that the production in 1939 amounted to 714,000,000 pounds, while in 1943 it jumped to 916,869,000 pounds. On the other hand the domestic disappearance of beef was seven per cent greater in 1943 than in 1939, while the situation is just the opposite in regard to pork. I suppose that results from the fact that more pork was exported. In 1939 we produced 679,968,000 pounds of pork, and in 1943 our production was 1,173,268,000 pounds. The percentage of exports jumped from 28-7 per cent in 1939 to 50-2 per cent in 1943. This is an interesting table, and I would ask the minister to give us a more detailed report from Colonel Robertson as to what is happening over there and what will be the effect on our future exports of agricultural products.

Of course it is not as easy now to get reports from the other side as it was before the war, and probably not as much can be gained from such reports, even though the amounts being shipped now are so much greater than those sent in peace time. Realizing, however, the necessity and importance of having such reports, we have sent for Colonel Robertson and I believe he is on his way back now. We want a complete review of the situation over there from him personally, in order that we may prepare for what will have to be done when the war ends. We have sent for him with that purpose in mind. At the moment I am afraid I have not a report from Colonel Robertson which would enable me to reply to what has been said.
Much of the information we have with regard to marketing over there does come from Colonel Robertson; and while I do not have a written report in regard to pork products I can say that we have exceeded our fondest hopes in connection with the marketing of pork products in Britain. Prior to the war, as I have said on former occasions, we hoped that we might get our exports to Britain up to something in the neighbourhood of 300,000,000 pounds a year, and that is what we were driving at. We were sending approximately that amount at the time war started. Last year, as hon. members know, we sent 675.000,000 pounds, and during the first six
Supply-Agriculture

months of this year we have sent 464,000,000 pounds. In other words, during the first six months of 1944 we have sent one and a half times as much as we had hoped to be able to send in the whole year before the war.
That is all meat products?

That is bacon and ham. At the time war started we had no hopes at all of being able to send any considerable quantity of beef to Britain. We sent from five or six thousand head of cattle a year to a high of thirty-eight thousand head, during the four or five years before the outbreak of war. In the early part of the war, as is indicated by the figtires just quoted, we were attempting to send over the greatest possible quantities of two products, bacon and cheese, and we did decrease our domestic consumption of cheese some years by denying our own people any cheese during the summer months. For two years, I think it was, all the cheese produced during the summer months was delivered to Britain, and the only cheese available for consumption in Canada' was that which we persuaded the cheese factories to make during the winter months.
As far as beef was concerned, during the first two years of the war we were selling all our surplus beef on the hoof to the United States. One year we sold in that market something like 200,000 head of cattle weighing 700 pounds or over. In 1942, however, as a result of taking so much pork off the market, we were eating all the beef available for consumption in Canada, and therefore discontinued shipping cattle to- the United States. During 1943, as a result of our urgings and also as a result of the fact that the farmers knew they had a market, the production of cattle increased materially. However, as hon. members know, it takes from two to three years to bring about an increase in the production of cattle, and that increased production just began to come on the market in the late fall of 1943. As a result we have sent to Britain, according to the latest report I have, some 55,000,000 pounds of beef, practically all of which has gone over since January 1 of this year, although a few hundred thousand pounds were sent in the last two or three months of 1943. That 55,000,000 pounds of beef represents something like 120,000 or 130,000 head of cattle. A considerable part of it has been in the form of boneless beef, which I think weighs out at something like 375 or 385 pounds a head. The carcasses sent over frozen would weigh between 450 and 500 pounds. If that is figured out it will be found that now' we are sending practiieally as many 
cattle to Great Britain in the form of beef as we were sending to the United States and Britain combined just before the war. That beef is being shipped in frozen form. Before the war we did not ship any quantity of beef in any form other than on the hoof. Hon. members will recall that in each session before the war I was questioned with respect to experiments I was carrying on. We were select-ting twenty-five head of wrhat we called baby beef each week, and shipping it to the Smith-field market.
We took it from as far west as Saskatoon and Calgary, shipping it in refrigerated cars from there to the wharves at Montreal and Saint John. Then we shipped it to the Smith-field market. We were able to land it there in about ten days' time. In Great Britain, of course, they consider beef ten days old as fresh beef. They believe in hanging it for ten days, before consuming it as fresh beef. Under proper conditions we are able to get it over there under ten days, and sell it on the Smithfield market. Our experience was that that beef topped the market, continuously, during the period of time we were carrying on those experiments. They were brought to an end by the war. It was impossible to ship that type of beef after the war started, and we did not have a sufficient volume of it in any event to make it worth while sending it. It cost us money to try that experiment.
It was baby beef.

Yes. Now we have an opportunity to demonstrate to the British that we have beef in Canada that can be sold, and if we can set up a market for Canadian frozen beef there is the possibility that when the war is over we may have a market in Great Britain for that product. We are working on it at the present time and, as I told the house the other day, we have an agreement extending over 1944 and 1945 under which the British are prepared to take all the beef in this condition we can send to them. They are providing us with the shipping with which to take it over.
Could the minister give us an estimate of what he thinks they will take in 1944, under the new contract?

All I can say is that we have covered a little better than six months of the contract, up to date, and we have sent over 55,000,000 pounds. That is more than half of what we have contracted to send in two years; I mean the minimum amount we have contracted to send in two years. If the marketing continues at the same pace we

Supply-Agriculture
should send them about four times that amount, or somewhere in the neighbourhood of 200,000,000 pounds.
The report I have in my hand says that last year we sent 44,000,000 pounds.
Where to?
To Great Britain.
No. There would not be 44,000,000 pounds last year. There is something wrong with that figure. That could not be millions of pounds.
Yes; to be exact, it is 44,122,042 pounds. That is what the report says.
The amount shipped last year was 15,000,000 pounds to all countries.

Mr. Chairman, the minister told the house yesterday or the day before, and repeated it tonight, about the contract for beef entered into. I suppose, with the British ministry of food. Will he tell the committee whether that contract was negotiated through his department or through the Department of Trade and Commerce?
Through my department.
Was it negotiated in Great Briain, or in New York with the British food board1?

It was really negotiated in Ottawa between representatives of the British food board who are in this City, and representatives of the Department of Agriculture. But there were communications back and forth before an agreement was finally reached.
The Department of Trade and Commerce did not enter into it at all?

The reason has been explained to the house before. I believe the Prime Minister on one occasion back in 1936 or 1937 stated clearly to the house the relationships existing between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture. He confined activities in connection with actual marketing in Canada to the Department of Agriculture. In all these contracts we deliver these products to the British at a Canadian port. In other words, all our bacon is delivered to the British at Saint John and Montreal-most of it at Saint John -and the British take the responsibility for it, from there on.
Of course that is not the condition in peace time. We are then under some responsibility to deliver the product in a certain form to
Great Britain. But in this period of war the British take delivery of it at a port in our country, and from there on it is their product; it is not ours.

The point I am trying to arrive at is this. I am trying to find out, if possible, whether the Department of Agriculture, through its trade commissioner or some other official, is taking over negotiating for the marketing of Canadian farm products on the British market. I should like to know just what these boards have to do with the matter. They certainly have something to do with it. Does the Department of Trade and Commerce enter into the negotiations at all?
No; they are all carried out through-
Then that means that the Department of Agriculture has taken over the marketing of agricultural products in Great Britain, at least for the period of the war?

No; it means exactly what I said, that right from the beginning of the war we have negotiated contracts, one of the reasons being that the two things are closely associated, namely, greater production and the shipping of production to Great Britain, and the other being that which I have just mentioned, namely, that we are delivering to Great Britain in Canada. These contracts have been made. The first was for bacon under the bacon board. The second was for cheese, under the dairy board. And the beef contract is made under the bacon board, now called the meat board. The beef contract is negotiated through the food board, with the advice of the meat board.
What about wheat?
The wheat is all handled by the wheat board.
And that is under the Department of Trade and Commerce?
Yes; it is under the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I was interested in the figures given a few minutes ago by the minister, when he went back to 1907. He gave us figures showing quantities of cheese exported from Canada to Great Britain, and the amount of cheese brought from New Zealand to Great Britain. In about thirty years those figures have almost reversed themselves. I believe there must have been some good reason for that, and I think the minister almost put his finger on the pulse of the trouble when he said that one could go down the Strand and see the products
Supply-Agriculture

of New Zealand and Australia advertised everywhere, but he could not see where the goods of Canada were advertised anywhere.
I remember being in London a few years ago; I may tell the committee that I searched all over the city of London to find Canadian goods, and the only place I saw the name of Canada was on Canada House. Yet we expect to maintain trade in a country, without even letting them know that there is a country such as Canada!
I walked down many of those streets and saw brilliantly lighted stores. One would see advertised in the windows of those stores, as far as the eye could reach, the products of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. But there was no such thing as that, so far as Canada was concerned. I am glad to note that an agricultural commissioner has been sent to London; in my view that is a step in the right direction. May I say I do not think the minister should allow this country ever to slip back to where we were in the last number of years. We should not allow the buyers of cheese, or the commission houses, to buy cheese f.o.b. Montreal for the old country market. We should see to it that our cheese is put in London, and that there is always a supply of Canadian cheese on hand over there to supply the market.
The fact that we did not do that was the reason why we lost our cheese market in the old country a few years ago. The simple fact was that New Zealand had in London warehouses filled with cheese at all times. When a storekeeper or merchant wanted cheese he simply telephoned to the commission house or wholesaler, and a supply of New Zealand cheese was delivered to him. But on many, many occasions there was no such supply of Canadian cheese.
I remember well an experience I had in a large hotel in London. I was having my dinner. The menu was presented to me, and on it I saw "Canadian cheese". I went out of my way to say to the waiter, "Is this Canadian cheese?" "Yes, sir", was the reply. The cheese was brought in to me and was served very nicely. It was cut in long narrow slabs and wrapped in cellophane. I tasted the cheese and immediately called the waiter and said, "I thought I asked you for Canadian cheese". "That is Canadian cheese", he said.
I said, "Send me the head waiter". The head waiter came and I said to him, "I asked for Canadian cheese which you are advertising on your menu, and this is what I got". He said, "That is Canadian cheese". I said, "Now I have a real complaint. Will you send in the manager". Presently the manager came in and I said, "You have Canadian cheese adver-

tised on your menu. I asked your waiter if you had it and he told me that you had, and this is what I got. Then I sent for the head waiter and complained that this was not Canadian cheese. I tell you that I am a Canadian and I know that this is not Canadian cheese". The manager said, "No, this is New Zealand cheese". I said, "Why do you serve me New Zealand cheese when I asked for Canadian cheese?" and he replied, "We cannot get a supply of Canadian cheese in London at all times and we are forced to buy from the supply which is always with us".
It may seem to be a little premature, but I believe that now is the time, when we have got our exports of cheese into the British market up to around 200,000,000 pounds a year, when we should lay a foundation for the post-war period. I think we should arrange to have in London a warehouse full of Canadian products at all times, so that our trade commissioner there can furnish a supply whenever there is a demand for it. But if we go back to the conditions of the old days we shall find in a very few years that we have lost that market. There is no doubt that we can hold that market if we look after it properly. We have the quality. We make the best cheese that is made in this world; there is no argument about that. But we must see to it that the supply is there when the demand is made for our products. We must see to it that our products are properly graded and that nothing but the best grades are sent to the British market. If we do not do that we cannot expect to compete in the markets of the world. New Zealand cheese, for example, can be produced more cheaply than Canadian cheese. It may be that the government of Canada should take up a little of the spread in order to see that the market for our Canadian cheese is maintained. The same thing applies to bacon. I had the privilege of eating bacon three times each day for four days when I was in Denmark and, Mr. Chairman, I am not prepared as a Canadian to admit that Danish bacon is equal in quality to [DOT] our first grade Canadian bacon. It is perhaps true that I was not furnished with the best grade bacon in Denmark, for the best grade of Danish bacon was sent to the British market. Just the reverse of that took place in the old days. We used to keep our first grade of bacon for consumption at home and send our inferior bacon to the British market, and then we wonder why we lost that market.

But late last fall many cheese factories in the country decided to remain open in the winter months and in many cases it has been the habit of farmers to ship their milk to cheese factories in the summer and to ship to the condensery plant in the fall and winter months because of the difference in price; and of course in the past there has been very little market for milk in cheese factories. If I remember correctly, he said that under that agreement the floor price for red and blue label beef would be twenty-five cents under the present ceiling price. What I mean is this: Will the producer be able to ship beef to the board, and the board take it over at the packing plant, kill that beef and have it credited, and the producer be paid on the basis of the grade, or is it just a guarantee to the packer that for any beef which he has within those grades he will receive twenty-five cents under the present ceiling price? I want to know how the government proposes to see that a fair price is carried back to the farmer?

It is exactly the same kind of agreement as we have with regard to hogs. We have not gone into the slaughtering business, and I do not think we intend to do so. We are buying the beef at any plant that can freeze it. It is not only a case of slaughtering it, the beef has to be frozen, and we buy the beef at the plant where it can be frozen, and have it shipped to Great Britain. The price we pay for that beef is twenty-five cents below the ceiling at the present time, and continues there until we have purchased the very considerable amounts mentioned.
The result of that is that a floor can be figured on what cattle w'ould sell at, at different points across Canada. In relation to that the department will do just what we have done in connection with hogs. We will keep a
check at all times on what is being paid on those markets. So far as hogs are concerned, we have had no reason to complain up to date, although we have been carrying on now for four or five years in connection with these contracts.
We think we shall have the same experience in connection with beef. As a matter of fact, cattle have been selling recently at above what would be called the price when beef is related to twenty-five cents below ceiling.
Is that the thin end of the wedge for the rail grading of beef?

It is not the thin end of the wedge for the rail grading of beef. That is not the intention of it at all, and probably it may not result in that. But I would say this, that in connection with the rail grading of beef, I doubt very much if anyone would undertake it until such time as the farmers are pretty well satisfied that they should have it. A large percentage were asking for it, before they got it in connection with hogs. Probably that is not true around Winnipeg, but in most other places it was.

The minister said that the meat board had found that so far as pork was concerned this ceiling price had worked out satisfactorily. I can agree with him on that. However, in connection with beef it has not worked out so satisfactorily. There has been greater variation in the price of beef to the consumer than there has been in the price of pork.
The minister said that his department was prepared to keep an eye on prices, and to see that prices of beef do not vary too widely, in accordance with floor prices. What action does the minister propose to take if the price
Supply-Agriculture

should drop below the floor, as it has on several occasions in the past two years? At those times the government have not taken any action; they have simply let the thing drag until it righted itself. The beef producers have at times accepted prices which were considerably below the floor.

As a matter of fact we discussed this whole question when the war estimates were before the committee. On that. occasion, after some considerable discussion with the hon. member for Lethbridge, who is not in his seat to-night, I stated to him that I did not think conditions existing in the last two years could be righted until such time as we had an agreement similar to the one I announced the other day.
The reason why there was more variation in prices was that we did not have an agreement of this kind, and we did not have a floor of the kind this agreement provides. The floor last year was a varying floor, and anticipated or made necessary varying prices. It started out at a quarter of a cent below the ceiling, and on August 20 or 27, I believe it was, dropped half a cent. Then it ran along for another month or so at that level, and dropped again. Finally, after three drops it went down to two and a quarter cents below the ceiling. Then, in the middle of December it started to rise again, and came up three-quarters of a cent. It then ran along until February, I believe it was, and came up another three-quarters of a cent. Then, finally, on May 27 it came up to the quarter of a cent below the ceiling again.
In other words, it was argued1 by people interested in the feeder lot handling of cattle that we should have a lower price in the fall, so that they could buy their cattle low, put them in feeder lots and 6011 them higher in the spring. We argued that that was not the proper way to handle cattle in war time, and that we should have a flat floor throughout the season. We said that we should have a floor on blue and1 red which would be fairly close to the ceiling, a floor on cows which would be a little farther away from the ceiling, and a floor on unfinished cattle which could be taken in and fed. Those would be plain cattle and other cattle which were not really fit for market, which could be taken in and fed up to the other grades, and sold when they were properly prepared for market.
That is provided for in This agreement, There is a flat floor on red and blue brand beef. There is a flat floor on cow beef, and a flat floor on plain and commercial grades below the cow beef standard. The result is 
that we think there will not be variation, just as there is not variation in hogs under this contract.

What will you do when the heavy run comes along in the fall, when there are all kinds of cattle from which to pick and choose? When you have a heavy run on the market you can pick out the good steers, and put them into blue and red beef. But if you take over a half-finished animal, where can you put him?
If you have a halffinished animal you can sell it as a feeder.
The packers will outbid you on that animal, and will take it and bone it. The man who is going to feed the steer will need that spread.

We have sufficient
spread, if it is the kind of animal my hon. friend is talking about. If it is an animal which is not properly fed or is not finished for the market, then of course both the packers and other people can buy it at wider spread than they can buy finished beef. We shall be in the market all the time for finished beef. We shall take all the finished beef that can be frozen and sent to Britain at any season of the year. That is the difference between conditions now and in peace time. In peace time when a rush of cattle came on the market in the fall there was no market for a certain percentage of them. As a result, feeders came and bought the cattle at one cent below the actual cattle price, based on beef, and they fed these cattle until they reached the red and blue class and then sold them at the beginning of the year as red and blue label beef. At the present time we can guarantee a market for all the finished beef, and there is only one difficulty in the way, but I must admit that it is a real difficulty. We must be able to get it through the plants that can freeze it. We have huge deliveries of hogs just as we have huge deliveries of cattle in the fall of the year, and there may be some difficulties unless the farmers will assist us by distributing their marketings over as long a period as possible rather than rushing them on to the market all at one time. We are hopeful that we shall be able to persuade them to assist us in the way I have suggested.
Are you going to have somebody on the market to buy these cattle in competition with the packers?

No; we are not buying cattle but beef, just as we are not buying hogs but bacon and ham.

You are buying only the two grades of beef?
No; we will buy cow beef as well.
I thought the minister said he was going to protect the market.
Certainly.

If the farmer does not get the price he wants he turns his cattle over to the abattoir where they are dressed on a rail-grade basis and then the government buys them. That is the way you protect the farmer.

I have not any brief for the packing plants, but I have not found them as crooked as some people think they are in our dealings with them. I quite agree that the packing plants want to make some money. Most people do. I find that even the C.C.F. when they are talking, usually talk about money, whether they can make enough to get by on. I have no doubt that the packing plants desire to make some money. On the other hand, we have found in our dealings with them during the war period that we have been able to maintain a flat price, or as near to a flat price as one can obtain under any system, from one end of the year to the other for hogs through the fact that we have made a deal with Britain under which we sell the surplus product to them and get delivery from the packing plants of the bacon. We have figured out the relationship between the price at which we sell to Britain and the price which the packing plants pay for the hogs; and we have been satisfied, as I believe the farmers themselves doing the marketing have been satisfied, that they are getting the best returns possible from their hogs in relation to the price at which the bacon and ham are sold.
We are satisfied that the same thing will happen in connection with beef. We are offering to buy not only the red and blue beef but cow beef at all times at a price which is three-quarters of a cent below the ceiling. We are also offering to buy the beef from the canners and the cutters and. that which is put into boneless beef at one cent and a quarter under the ceiling. We will buy that at all times unless somebody else is prepared to pay more for it. The only way in which the trade will get that beef is to pay more than we are prepared to pay for it. If any packer does not pay enough for the cattle, some other packer will compete with him and the competition will go on between them. They can establish a proper price level for all the cattle that the farmers deliver on that market.
We are hopeful that the farmers will cooperate in this. It is much better for the farmers to keep cattle that are not properly fed back in the farming districts rather than send them into Winnipeg, where feeders near Winnipeg will take them out, feed them up and then put them back on the market. We think it is better for the farmers to keep their cattle back in the farming districts until they are finished. That will help in handling the cattle both in the stockyards and through the plants in the rush seasons of the year.

I was very glad to hear the minister make the announcement that he did on Friday last, but I am sorry that the farmer or producer is not protected. As I have said before, a year ago, before the agriculture committee we were given to understand that protection would be given to the farmer, but so far I do not see anything of that kind being done because prices paid by the packers are not always what they should be. Under this programme the packer is guaranteed his price and his profits; but the farmer, when he brings his cattle on the market, is still at the mercy of the packer. The farmers are not organized as the packers are. I realize that that is the fault of the farmers themselves. For that reason the announcement of the minister is very much in favour of the packers. I should be very glad to see the government go on the market and buy live cattle rather than allow prices to go down to where they have gone on several occasions in past years. If what I suggest were done, instead of it being left to the packers to set the prices, the farmers would be guaranteed something worth while under the announcement made by the minister.

I have just one comment to make. I was surprised to hear the minister state that the government was prepared to buy not only red and blue label beef but also cows and other unfinished cattle which were perhaps not of good conformation. We have been trying our best to provide the best bacon possible for the British market because we want to keep up the reputation of our bacon in England. I am afraid that if we start shipping inferior quality of beef to that market we are going to lose the market which we might otherwise gain and keep. I was sorry to hear the minister state that he is prepared to buy poor quality beef and even boneless and send it to Britain, because everyone knows that the poorer qualities of cattle will not produce the first-rate beef which the Britisher enjoys. A beef type of animal of good conformation puts his flesh on the parts where the high price cuts come from; but the poorer

qualities, some of our dairy cattle, do not dc that, and the beef is naturally not as good. I hope that the minister will reconsider and not send too much poor quality beef into the British market.

On one or two former occasions I intimated that I should like to say a word or two in reference to this vote when it came before the committee, because in the last couple of years I have had the pleasure and profit of examining a goodly portion of the work which has been done by the prairie farm rehabilitation board. I am glad to say that to my mind one of the best pieces of legislation passed through this house at any time-I have no notion at the moment, by which government-was the legislation which pertains to the prairie farm rehabilitation board. Last summer I looked over quite a number of the dugouts which have been made by the board, one or two of the very small irrigation projects, and a number of stock-watering dams. The board deserves unstinted praise for the work it has achieved. I am not passing any comment upon the cost; I am speaking only about the work which has been done, to which I just referred. The last figures I could obtain are as of 1943, and show that altogether in 1943 alone there have been completed over a thousand projects, divided into three divisions, dugouts, stockwatering dams and small irrigation projects. When the minister replies to what I have to say I should like him to tell us whether the department plans to quadruple or increase by five, six, eight or ten times the amount of this vote as soon as it can possibly do so. As a business man I cannot figure why the vote has not been larger and larger every year; the results obtained from what has been done have been so splendid. They are self-liquidating projects, and since they have achieved a great deal, why not greatly multiply the vote?
I found the board's work in two of the provinces. I did not see any of it in Manitoba, because I was not in the southwest part of the province, where I believe they have control. In Saskatchewan they have done good work and have planned more good work, but I should like to know from the minister why any delay has occurred in carrying out the plans which the prairie farm rehabilitation board have made for southern Alberta. Every dollar spent in carrying out the projects planned for southern Alberta would be self-liquidating and give ample returns. I believe the board have prepared plans for building a dam on the St. Mary river at Spring Coulee. Why not bring in a vote and proceed with it? The minister knows better than any other hon. member that unless the dam at Spring Coulee is proceeded with we stand in jeopardy of losing our allotted flow from the St. Mary river. We cannot forever let it run to waste when our cousins to the south can use it. Therefore I should like the minister, at some

Supply-Agriculture
time, not now but at some later session if he is then in control of the department, to bring in a vote to provide for the building of a dam at Spring Coulee on the St. Mary river, so that southern Alberta can obtain the water for much needed irrigation works.
I cannot understand why the vote now being asked for is so small. Two million dollars will not go very far, and if you examine the table on page 69 of the estimates you will observe that the money is distributed under quite a number of headings, such as salaries and wages, cost of living bonus, equipment-I assume that "equipment" refers to machinery and so forth to be used by men working under the prairie farm administration board-freight, express and cartage, miscellaneous, printing and stationery, rents, telephones, telegrams and postage, travelling expenses. The only money I see which is directly allocated to building works is S621.000 under the heading "buildings and lands"; perhaps also $113,000 under "supplies and materials." Together they amount to only $734,000. I should like the minister to tell the committee why, when the results have been so splendid, a much larger amount is not asked for.
Is any of this vote to be used in connection with the water requirements of Regina? I noticed in the paper a few days ago, as probably the minister also did, a statement by the city superintendent of waterworks, Mr. J. W. D. Farrell, in which he tells in a few words the situation. He pointed out that they obtained their water from three sources- Mound springs, Mallory springs, and Boggy creek-and stated that the capacity of those three sources of supply amount to five and one-half million gallons a day. The population of Regina at present is around sixty thousand. Including the immediate suburbs, part of which are comprised, I believe, in the constituency of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I do not think I shall be far out in surmising that Regina has to supply approximately sixty-five thousand people with water. That provides for a comparatively small gallonage per capita for a city of that size. Perhaps a year or more ago we had a fire in Toronto, not a fire of any particular size, at Lyons' Furniture company's store on Yonge street.
It took 750,000 gallons of water to subdue that fire, and it was only a medium one. What would Regina do if it required 750,000 gallons to put out a fire? And it might have three or four fires of that extent. I appeal to the minister not to be afraid to give that city and the adjacent city of Moose Jaw fair play. I am afraid he is too timid, too humble in asking for fair play for his province, asking for that to which it is entitled. It would be a disaster if the waterworks of Regina were called upon to put up a million and a half or two million gallons in one day to subdue a fire, and that would not be a particularly large fire. Are we fair in placing that city in jeopardy like that, particularly when we have the engineers under the prairie farm rehabilitation board to assist. I will not cover what I said before, but knowing from investigation the position in those cities from the point of view of water supply I once again ask the minister to press for whatever sized vote is necessary to provide adequate protection for those two cities.
In Toronto I have seen water mains burst, and I have no doubt other hon. members here have been in that city when some water mains have given way. The hon. member for York South is likely familiar with the bursting of a large water main that goes up Bathurst street. What causes such things is a weakness in the water main. Well, what would happen in Regina if during a fire of any magnitude, a twelve, or fifteen or twenty-inch water main burst? The amount of water that would be lost from that main before the situation could be got under control might mean disaster. A few days ago the minister read the statement of the superintendent of the Regina water department in which it is pointed out that their maximum apparently is 5,500,000 gallons a day, when a city of that size, using the same amount of water per person as is used in Ottawa, would require over 7,000,000 gallons a day without any allowance for extra demand for great fires. I am sure the minister would have the support of the house as well as the country if he asked for whatever amount might be required to ensure that the capital of his own province as well as the adjacent city of Moose Jaw be given that protection which is their right. The people of the country placed that capital -where it is and they started its growth and the growth of the other city, but neither of those centres can properly develop under these circumstances. Regina has a population of 60,000 whereas it should have from 80,000 to 100,000. If it were guaranteed a water supply I am sure its industry would expand. The industry that I was in for many years, the radiator and boiler industry, requires a great deal of water. Could anyone start such an industry in Regina or Moose Jaw? It is an industry that consumes a large volume of water. If I wanted to start such a plant in Regina one of my first acts would be to visit the city hall to ascertain how much water I could have, how many thousand gallons per

day; but what would they tell me, when they are now delivering per capita so much less than eastern cities?
I do not wish to labour the subject, but I suggest that the minister is not putting enough emphasis on the water situation in those two cities. Again I say he is too humble, not vigorous enough in this matter, although he has plenty of vigour when he gets his dander up. I want to see him get his dander up. I want him to get his back up and ask for whatever is fair in order t-o place those two cities in a satisfactory position of defence against what I hope will never happen but what might happen. The matter comes under this vote, and if it does, then $2,000,000 is a mere bagatelle. The minister should ask for $20,000,000. It would create business. He need not ask for it all in one year, but he should ask for sufficient to make an adequate start in order to give those western cities and the adjacent municipalities a chance to go forward and provide a defence against any possible contingency.

This is an important item, and I notice there is no increase this year. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has pleaded with the minister to consider assistance for the city of Regina, and I presume he includes Moose Jaw. Recently the hon. member has received a telegram from the mayors of those cities asking him to bring the matter to the attention, I presume, of the Minister of Agriculture or some other member of the government, and asking also that he solicit the support of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross).
I would rather have the minister's support.

I happened to see a copy of the telegram askng him to try to get their support for a project of this kind, and he has brought it to-night forcibly to the attention of the minister. The hon. gentleman has spoken many times in this house on matters pertaining to water power and development, water supply and other projects in Saskatchewan, and he has made a point of touring the district in the last two or three years, so that he knows the situation as well as any hon. member coming from that province does. We all appreciate his efforts, and there is no doubt about it that, from reading the press, the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta appreciate the interest the hon. member has taken in these matters. The bill setting up this branch of the department was passed1 in 1934.
It was 1935.
This is the eighth year of the operation of the act.
The date is April 17, 1935.

At any rate, the idea was to provide a water supply to certain parts of Saskatchewan and the west. Since that time and under the direction of the present minister this department has developed and taken on many other projects of one kind and another. I notice from the report that there are four or five cultural activities, water developments, small individual projects, community projects and larger projects. Then there is land utilization and land settlement. The hon. member who has just spoken referred to some of them. I notice that large water projects to the number of fifty-eight were provided for in the irrigation scheme. The minister should explain the different branches of this work of water development. For instance, he should deal with community pastures and give us a detailed statement with respect to each one, what they did last year and what they proposed to do this year.
I notice that on page 69 of the estimates there is a column on the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, but there is no list of the employees such as there is in the other branches of the department. You can get a detailed statement of the employees this year and last year for the other branches of the department, but there is no list of the employees of these projects. Reviewing the details of the item we find that three items alone, salaries, wages, cost of living bonus and other payments including travelling expenses amount to $1,012,000. These three items alone amount to more than half of the total vote. I think the minister should give us a list of the employees and inspectors in each one of those branches or projects that I have mentioned. He should tell us whether the employees have increased in numbers this year. He should give us the total number of employees and whether there has been an increase in the last six months, and, if so, in what Way. I have covered four or five of the different projects undertaken at one time instead of taking each one individually. I think the minister should give us a more detailed statement than we have in the estimate or in the report on last year's work.

In answer to the latter part of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle I would call his attention to the fact that on or about February 28, 1944, I answered a question asked by Mr. Douglas of Weyburn, giving the names and addresses of the fieldmen in Saskatchewan. The question was made an order for return, and I do not think he would expect me to go over it again. It can be looked up under that date. I have them here in my hand. There is a long list of them.
Is there any increase in the last two months?

Just the engineers that are taken on for the season. We make up our engineering staffs that go out with some rod men and others who are necessary to the making up of those engineering staffs to do the inspection work.
On the question of the vote, the vote is $2,000,000. I would, of course, call the attention of the hon. member for Davenport to the fact that when I came to Ottawa the limitation on that vote was $1,000,000 a year. It was a vote of $4,750,000 which was to be expended as follows: not more than $750,000 the first year and not more than $1,000,000 a year in the succeeding years. As the act then stood it came to an end at the end of five years. It was an act for the purpose of taking care of what was looked upon as a temporary condition brought about by drought, and was to be utilized for that purpose. When I came to Ottawa I insisted that this was a job which would take at least twenty years and could not be done in less time than that no matter how much money was provided, and that no system under which you provided only $1,000,000 a year could possibly take care of it.
Could you not ask for more?

I did ask for more. As a matter of fact, the first year I had quite a time in getting the bill through this house, largely because of opposition coming from directly opposite; but I asked to have the vote under the bill enlarged and made so that I could spend any amount of money that I could persuade the house to vote for me in any session. I finally got it through. As a matter of fact I had to bring it back the second time before I could get it through the house in the form desired. I did not get it entirely changed the first year. I managed to get the amount out the first year, I think, or the dates out, or vice versa. But I had to come back the second time in order to get it enlarged to the extent it is now. As a result of those activities we got the amount increased year by year, until finally in 1938-39 it was up to $3,500,000, but the second $500,000 was voted only on condition that it was expended on some particular project, one of them being the project that had to do with supplying water to Moose Jaw and another in the form of supplying stationary water at Saskatoon. But it took considerable discussion in the house to get those votes agreed to. In two years before the war we got up to $3,500,000. It was cut by a quarter of a million in the year before the war, that is 1939-40, the reason being that about half of the amount of money that was set up for conservation of water supply in those larger projects was not voted in the second year; only the amount that had not been expended in the preceding year was allowed in the second year. When the war started that vote was cut. In 1939-40 it was cut to $3,250,000; in 1940-41 it was cut to $2,500,000; in 1941-42, we retained the same amount. In 1942-43 it was cut to $2,000,000, and in 1943-44, it was $2,000,000, making a total of $19,684,420.69. But I repeat that even now it is twice as large as could possibly be spent under the act as it stood when I came to Ottawa in 1935. I say that in order to impress upon the committee that this act was set up for the purpose of doing a particular job. When it was set up by the previous government in 1935 it had no relationship whatsoever to problems such as that which confronts the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw.
It was only after getting a special vote of something like $500,000 in the first instance and another $100,000 later on, that we wore able to do anything in connection with the Moose Jaw situation; and it will be noted that this was taken care of by the special phraseology of the item put in the year in

That is taken up in the construction of such works as pastures, for example. A foreman goes out and hires farmers living in a community to go on the job and build a fence around, for instance, 50,000 acres of land. In some cases it would be 100.000 acres of land. Those fences are constructed and then, in addition to that, they provide water supplies. _ It may be a matter of putting up a windmill, or it may be a matter of digging dugouts, or it may be a matter of putting in dams. However, it would be something necessary to the conservation of a water supply for the watering of stock on the pastures.
That is all included in wages, but it is all actual work being done for the purpose of carrying out the intentions of the act. One could go through the different items, and say that is what happens in connection with them. Expenditures are not made only on the hiring of people to go round the country to run up expense accounts. There are a certain number who have to have expense accounts, but they are not the big items.

What number of dugouts
have been supplied this year since April 1? Also, what number of survey parties have been working during the summer?

There were 1,307 built last year, with the same vote we have this year, and over 1,400 the year before. I am informed that the vote was practically exhausted by the middle of July, and that
